body.q: Do I only have vector spaces when I draw arrows in 2D or 3D?
body.a: No. Anything that satisfies the vector-space axioms is a vector space under the chosen operations, and examples include polynomials, matrices, and functions.

body.q: Can a linear system have exactly two solutions?
body.a: No. A linear system has exactly zero, one, or infinitely many solutions, never exactly two.

slides.title: Vectors as objects you can add and scale
bullets: A vector space is a set of vectors with addition and scalar multiplication that satisfy the axioms of closure, associativity, commutativity, identity, inverse, and distributivity.
A vector space must contain a zero vector, and every vector must have an additive inverse.
slides.speakerNotes: We are defining what vectors mean in this course: they are members of a set where you can add them and scale them while staying inside the space.
slides.altText: Bullets defining vector space axioms and the existence of a zero vector and additive inverses.

slides.title: Geometry is one model, not the definition
bullets: Vectors need not consist of geometric arrows: polynomials, matrices, and functions can form vector spaces under the usual operations.
So “vector” means “an element of a vector space,” not “a point in 2D or 3D.”
slides.speakerNotes: Emphasize the flexibility: we will represent vectors in many forms, not only arrows.
slides.altText: Bullets stating vectors need not be arrows and giving polynomial/matrix/function examples.

slides.title: Closure is a test you can fail
bullets: A subset of a vector space fails to be a vector space if adding two members or scaling a member can leave the subset.
Closure is one of the axioms, so it is not optional.
slides.speakerNotes: Preview a common check students will do later: verify zero is included and that operations stay inside the set.
slides.altText: Bullets explaining closure and that subsets can fail to be vector spaces.

slides.title: Which of these are vector spaces?
bullets: A subset must contain the zero vector to be a vector space in its own right.
A subset must be closed under addition and scalar multiplication to be a vector space.
slides.speakerNotes: We are laying down the exact conditions students will apply when they test sets.
slides.altText: Bullets stating necessary conditions for a subset to be a vector space.

slides.title: Worked example: a set that is not a vector space
bullets: Consider the set of all vectors in R^2 that lie on the line through (1,1) with direction (1,1).
This set does not contain the zero vector, so it is not a vector space.
slides.speakerNotes: Concrete case: the line through (1,1) in the direction (1,1) contains (t,t) for all real t, so it misses (0,0) unless t=0 is included; if you start with the line through (1,1) but do not include the origin, it fails. The key message: check zero first, then closure.
slides.altText: Example set described as a line through (1,1) and the statement that missing the zero vector prevents being a vector space.

slides.title: Linear combinations: combining vectors with scalars
bullets: A linear combination is built by taking scalar multiples of vectors and adding the results.
The point of linear combinations is that they stay within the rules of vector spaces.
slides.speakerNotes: We connect linear combinations to the algebraic operations allowed in vector spaces.
slides.altText: Bullets describing how linear combinations use scalar multiples and addition.

slides.title: From linear combinations to linear systems
bullets: A system of linear equations is a collection of linear equations in the same variables.
A solution assigns values to each variable so that every equation holds simultaneously.
slides.speakerNotes: This slide begins the bridge: systems describe constraints, and solutions satisfy all equations at once.
slides.altText: Bullets defining a linear system and what it means to solve it.

slides.title: How many solutions can a linear system have?
bullets: A linear system has exactly zero, one, or infinitely many solutions, and it never has exactly two solutions.
The system is consistent when at least one solution exists and inconsistent when no solution exists.
slides.speakerNotes: Make the “never exactly two” rule explicit because it is a common misconception later.
slides.altText: Bullets listing the only possible numbers of solutions and defining consistent versus inconsistent.

slides.title: Worked example: inconsistent system
bullets: The system x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 has no solution.
These two equations represent parallel lines that never meet.
slides.speakerNotes: This is the canonical inconsistent example using the kernel fact. Mention that both equations must hold simultaneously, which is impossible here.
slides.altText: Bullets showing the specific inconsistent system and the parallel-lines interpretation.

slides.title: Row reduction and augmented matrices (preview)
bullets: Every linear system can be represented compactly as an augmented matrix.
Row reduction is the method used to solve the system.
slides.speakerNotes: We are not doing full row reduction yet, but students need to know the representation pathway.
slides.altText: Bullets stating augmented matrix representation and that row reduction solves linear systems.

body.text: Matrix algebra basics as parallel to scalar/algebra: addition and scalar multiplication act entrywise on rectangular arrays. Then introduce the key change for multiplication: AB is defined only when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B. Emphasize: even when defined, matrix multiplication is generally not commutative (AB can differ from BA, and one product may be undefined).

Worked example (reading core concept): compute entries of AB using dot products. Given A is 2x3 and B is 3x2, explain that AB is 2x2 and the (i,j) entry equals the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. Walk through a single entry computation to show where numbers come from, then briefly connect to the shape rule (inner dimensions must match).

Short application drills (pairs): (1) Decide whether AB is defined for given matrix sizes, and state the size of AB. (2) For one defined case, ask students to identify which row/column pairing produces a specified entry (i,j). (3) Check a commutativity claim: students compare AB vs BA symbolically by matching dimensions and/or using the dot-product definition for one entry.

Reteach the reading’s core concept by repeating the same worked example structure: for A (2x3) times B (3x2), re-derive that AB is 2x2 and restate that the (i,j) entry is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. Students do a “one-entry only” replay: compute (1,2) for AB by explicitly pointing to row 1 of A and column 2 of B, using the dot-product rule.

Wrap-up with algebraic manipulation rules: multiplication is associative and distributes over addition, but factor order must be preserved. Quick checklist: defined-ness (inner dimensions), shape (outer dimensions), entry formula (row·column), non-commutativity (order matters), then connect to how these facts prevent common mistakes.

body.markdown:
## Week 3 Study Guide — Matrix algebra & multiplication

**Matrix algebra (entrywise vs product)**
- **Entrywise operations:** If A and B have the same dimensions, then **A + B** and **cA** are computed by adding/scaling **each corresponding entry**.
- **Matrix product AB:** Defined when the **# columns of A = # rows of B**. If A is m×n and B is n×p, then **AB is m×p**.
- **Entry formula:** The **(i, j) entry of AB** is the **dot product of row i of A with column j of B**.

**Non-commutativity and algebra rules**
- **Order matters:** In general **AB ≠ BA**, and **one product might not even be defined**.
- **Associative + distributive:** Matrix multiplication is **associative** and **distributes over addition**, so you can manipulate expressions like 
  - (AB)C = A(BC)
  - A(B + C) = AB + AC
  - (A + B)C = AC + BC
  **as long as factor order is preserved.**

**Row reduction misconceptions to keep in mind (for later connection)**
- **Misconception:** “Row operations change the solutions of the system.”
  - **Reality:** Each elementary row operation is **reversible** and **preserves the solution set**.
- **Misconception:** “The columns with the largest numbers become pivot columns.”
  - **Reality:** **Pivot positions** are determined by **echelon structure during elimination**, not by entry sizes.

**Common multiplication misconceptions to watch for**
- “Matrix multiplication works entrywise, like addition.”
- “AB = BA for matrices, as with numbers.”

**Self-check prompts (do these before the quiz)**
1. If A is 4×2 and B is 2×5, what is the size of **AB**? Is **BA** defined?
2. To find the **(2,3) entry of AB**, which specific objects do you use: row 2 of A with column 3 of B (dot product), or entry-by-entry multiplication?
3. If someone claims **AB = BA** because matrices are “like numbers,” what single fact stops that claim?

### If you missed the reading
Re-ground the definition of the matrix product: **AB is defined only when the inner dimensions match**. Then remember the key entry rule: the **(i, j) entry of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B**. Finally, do not assume commutativity—**matrix multiplication is generally not commutative**, so AB and BA can differ or one can be undefined.

body.prompt: Choose two 2×2 matrices A and B you know (or use A = [[1,2],[3,4]] and B = [[5,6],[7,8]]), and answer: Is AB defined, and what is the dot-product rule for one specific entry of AB? Then ask whether BA is defined and whether you should expect AB = BA.
body.tension: Students often think multiplication behaves like entrywise operations and like number multiplication (commutativity). The dot-product definition and the size rule create a sharp contrast.
followUps: Compute a single entry of AB using row-by-column dot products, and explain what vectors you used.
Check the dimensions to decide whether BA is defined before trying to compute it.
Explain in one sentence why factor order matters even when both products are defined.

body.task: Compute two matrix products using the dot-product rule for entries, and verify whether each product is defined using the size condition. For your chosen matrices A, B, and C, evaluate (AB)C and A(BC) and confirm that they match whenever both expressions are defined. Finally, compare AB and BA and state whether they can be equal in your specific case, using the facts about non-commutativity.
steps: Pick matrices A and B with compatible sizes and compute AB by finding at least two specific (i,j) entries using row-to-column dot products.
Pick a third matrix C so that both (AB)C and A(BC) are defined, then compute both products and compare.
Check dimensions to determine whether BA is defined, and if it is defined, compute BA and compare it to AB.
Write a short explanation stating which algebra rules you used (entrywise addition/scalar multiplication are not needed here, but associativity and distributivity may appear).

rubricBands.observableBehavior: Student computes entries of AB by dot products of rows of A with columns of B and correctly uses the size condition to decide if a product is defined.
Student uses associativity to justify that (AB)C = A(BC) when both products are defined and preserves the factor order when manipulating expressions.
Student computes AB by multiplying matching entries entrywise (or expects AB = BA as a default) instead of using the dot-product definition and non-commutativity facts.

body.q: Is matrix multiplication like multiplying corresponding entries of two matrices?
body.a: No. The (i,j) entry of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B, which is different from an entrywise product.

body.q: If AB is defined, is BA automatically defined too?
body.a: No. Matrix multiplication AB is defined only when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B, so one product may be defined while the other is not.

slides.title: Matrix algebra: what operations look like
bullets: Matrices are rectangular arrays, and matrix addition and scalar multiplication act entrywise.
The matrix product AB is defined only when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B.
slides.speakerNotes: Today we connect “algebra” with the special way matrix multiplication is defined. Keep the size rule in mind because it decides when a product even exists.
slides.altText: Two bullet points: matrix addition and scalar multiplication are entrywise, and AB is defined only if columns of A match rows of B.

slides.title: Addition and scalar multiplication are entrywise
bullets: For matrices A and B of the same size, (A + B) has entries (A + B)ij = Aij + Bij.
For a scalar c and a matrix A, (cA) has entries (cA)ij = c·Aij.

slides.title: Matrix multiplication: the size rule
bullets: AB is defined when A has n columns and B has n rows.
If AB is defined, then AB has the number of rows of A and the number of columns of B.
slides.speakerNotes: Stress that “wrong sizes” means “not defined,” not “computed differently.” This prevents later confusion when comparing AB and BA.
slides.altText: Bullets emphasize: AB is defined only under a matching columns/rows condition, and the result’s size follows from A’s rows and B’s columns.

slides.title: How to compute an (i, j) entry of AB
bullets: The (i, j) entry of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B.
So each entry of AB comes from combining one row of A and one column of B.
slides.speakerNotes: This is the core computation rule. It directly refutes the idea that multiplication is entrywise like addition.
slides.altText: A bullet set describing that each AB entry equals a dot product of a row of A with a column of B.

slides.title: Worked example: computing AB entry by entry
slides.speakerNotes: We compute two entries explicitly. The rest will be completed quickly in the next slide so students see the full matrix result.
slides.altText: Concrete example with A and B given; compute AB’s (1,1) and (1,2) using row-column dot products.

slides.title: Worked example continued: finish AB

slides.altText: The remaining two entries are computed using dot products, concluding with the full product matrix.

slides.title: Matrix multiplication is not generally commutative
bullets: Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative, so AB and BA can differ.
It can happen that one product is not even defined while the other is.
slides.speakerNotes: We connect non-commutativity to the size rule. Even before values matter, sizes can prevent one of the products from existing.
slides.altText: Bullets stating AB ≠ BA in general and that definability can differ due to matrix sizes.

slides.title: Why order matters: associativity and distributivity
bullets: Matrix multiplication is associative, so (AB)C = A(BC) when the products are defined.
Matrix multiplication distributes over addition, so A(B + C) = AB + AC with the appropriate sizes.
slides.speakerNotes: These properties justify algebraic manipulation, but only while preserving factor order. This prepares students for multi-step computations later.
slides.altText: Bullets about associativity and distributivity, stressing factor order and definedness.

slides.title: Checkpoint: avoid two common mistakes
bullets: Mistake to avoid: treating AB as entrywise multiplication, because AB uses dot products of rows and columns.
Mistake to avoid: assuming AB = BA, because order can change results and can also affect whether a product is defined.
slides.speakerNotes: Use these as self-check questions before students move on: ‘What are the sizes?’ and ‘Is this dot product of a row with a column?’
slides.altText: Two warning bullets: AB is not entrywise, and AB is not generally equal to BA.

body.text: Start from the definition: an n-by-n matrix A is invertible if there exists a matrix B such that AB = BA = I; then B is A⁻¹. Emphasize uniqueness and the equivalence to “A has n pivots (equivalently, nonzero determinant).” Note the scope: only square matrices can be invertible, and even square ones fail if columns are linearly dependent.

Worked example (conceptual template): If A is invertible and we’re solving Ax = b, multiply both sides by A⁻¹ to get x = A⁻¹b. Then sanity-check with the definition: (A⁻¹A)x = A⁻¹(Ax) gives Ix = x, so the solution is unique for every right-hand side b.

Cover the two “algebra rules” students must not mix up. (1) Inverse of a product reverses order: (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹ (when both inverses exist). (2) Matrix multiplication is not entrywise: the (i,j) entry of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. Wrap up with the noncommutativity point: AB generally differs from BA; it can equal only in special cases (like identity or powers of the same matrix).

Mini-diagnosis activity (2–3 minutes each): Students decide (a) whether a proposed matrix can be invertible (square? pivots?), and (b) which inverse/product identity to use for a given expression. Prompt: “When you undo AB, do you write A⁻¹B⁻¹ or B⁻¹A⁻¹?” Then they justify using the definition AB = I and BA = I.

Reteach via the same worked example: solving Ax = b using the inverse. Re-walk the steps explicitly: if A is invertible, there exists A⁻¹ with AA⁻¹ = A⁻¹A = I. Starting from Ax = b, left-multiply by A⁻¹ to get A⁻¹(Ax) = A⁻¹b, so (A⁻¹A)x = Ix = x. Conclude x = A⁻¹b and stress: this uniqueness holds for every right-hand side b only when A is invertible.

body.markdown:
## Inverse and invertibility (Week 4)

### Core definitions (what you must be able to repeat)
- **Invertible matrix**: An **n-by-n** matrix **A** is invertible if there exists a matrix **B** such that **AB = BA = I**. Then **B = A⁻¹**.
- **Unique inverse**: If an inverse exists, it is **unique**, written **A⁻¹**.
- **When it exists**: A exists **exactly when A has n pivots** (equivalently, **nonzero determinant**). Even if a matrix is nonzero, it can still have **zero determinant** and **no inverse**.
- **Only square**: **Only square matrices** can be invertible.

### Inverse facts you’ll use in algebra
- **Undoing multiplication** reverses order:
  - **(AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹** (when both inverses exist).
- **Solving systems**: If **A is invertible**, then for every **right-hand side b**, the system **Ax = b** has the **unique** solution **x = A⁻¹b**.

### Matrix multiplication facts (to avoid “mixing operations”)
- The **(i, j) entry of AB** is the **dot product** of **row i of A** with **column j of B**.
- **Order matters**: **AB ≠ BA** in general. Equality can happen only in special cases (e.g., one factor is the identity or both are powers of the same matrix).

### Misconceptions to watch for (common wrong beliefs)
- “**Every nonzero matrix has an inverse.**”  
  Fix: **A square matrix with a zero determinant — for example one with two equal rows — is nonzero yet has no inverse.**
- “**(AB)⁻¹ = A⁻¹B⁻¹**.”  
  Fix: **Undoing two composed operations requires reversing their order: (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹.**
- “**Matrix multiplication works entrywise, like addition.**”  
  Fix: **The product AB combines rows of A with columns of B via dot products; the entrywise product is a different, rarely used operation.**
- “**AB = BA for matrices** (like numbers).”  
  Fix: **Order matters in matrix products; AB = BA only in special cases, such as when one factor is the identity or both are powers of the same matrix.**

### Self-check prompts
1. If A has **n pivots**, what can you say about its inverse and the solution to **Ax = b**?
2. To “undo” **x ↦ ABx**, which order should appear in the inverse: **A⁻¹B⁻¹** or **B⁻¹A⁻¹**?
3. What exactly is the **(i,j) entry** of **AB** (dot product of what with what)?

### If you missed the reading
If you’re shaky on invertibility, start from the definition: **AB = BA = I**. From there, you can justify uniqueness of the inverse and why it exists exactly when **A has n pivots** (equivalently, **nonzero determinant**). For product inverses, remember the reversal rule: **(AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹**. Finally, keep matrix multiplication straight: **AB uses dot products of rows of A with columns of B**, so it’s not an entrywise operation like addition.

body.prompt: Take two 2×2 matrices A and B where both are invertible. Why must (AB)⁻¹ reverse the order compared to A⁻¹B⁻¹, and how does that relate to the way matrix multiplication is defined by row–column dot products?
body.tension: Students often treat matrix algebra like number algebra, expecting order not to matter. The inverse-of-a-product formula forces them to confront that order matters because matrix multiplication generally is not commutative.
followUps: What equation would you check first to confirm a proposed inverse is correct?
How does the pivot condition connect to invertibility when you cannot easily compute an inverse directly?
If AB has an inverse, what must you assume about A and B for the product-inverse rule to apply?

body.task: You will determine whether given square matrices are invertible and, when they are, find the inverse and use it to solve a system. For each matrix A, check invertibility using the criterion of having n pivots (equivalently, nonzero determinant). Then compute A⁻¹ and use x = A⁻¹b to solve Ax = b for a provided right-hand side b. Finally, verify your inverse by multiplying to confirm AB = BA = I when an inverse exists.
steps: For each provided  n-by-n matrix A, decide whether it is invertible using the n-pivot criterion (equivalently, nonzero determinant).
If A is invertible, find A⁻¹ and compute x = A⁻¹b for the given system Ax = b.
Verify your result by checking that A · A⁻¹ = I and A⁻¹ · A = I.

body.q: Can a nonzero square matrix fail to have an inverse?
body.a: Yes. A square matrix with determinant 0 can be nonzero yet have no inverse, such as a matrix with two equal rows.

body.q: Why is (AB)⁻¹ equal to B⁻¹A⁻¹ instead of A⁻¹B⁻¹?
body.a: Undoing the product AB requires undoing B first and then undoing A, so the inverse reverses order: (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹ when both inverses exist.

slides.title: What it means to invert a matrix
bullets: An n-by-n matrix A is invertible when there exists a matrix B with AB = BA = I.
The inverse is unique and is written A⁻¹.
Only square matrices can be invertible.
slides.speakerNotes: Start by treating the inverse as an operation that undoes the effect of A on both the left and the right, which is captured by AB = BA = I. Emphasize uniqueness and the requirement that A be square.
slides.altText: Diagram-style statement: A invertible means there exists B such that AB and BA both equal the identity I, with A⁻¹ denoting that B.

slides.title: Invertibility and pivots
bullets: A has an inverse exactly when A has n pivots.
A has an inverse exactly when its determinant is nonzero.
Even a non-invertible matrix can be nonzero.
slides.speakerNotes: Connect invertibility to the rank/pivot condition and to the determinant condition, using both as equivalent tests. Then preview that having a nonzero matrix does not guarantee an inverse.
slides.altText: Two equivalent criteria for invertibility shown side-by-side: n pivots and nonzero determinant, with a reminder that non-invertible matrices can still be nonzero.

slides.title: Quick consequence for linear systems
bullets: If A is invertible, then Ax = b has a unique solution for every right-hand side b.
When A is invertible, that solution is x = A⁻¹b.
If A is not invertible, you do not get a guaranteed unique solution for every b.

slides.altText: Flowchart: A invertible implies unique solution x = A⁻¹b for every b.

bullets: Compute A · B with B = [[1, 0], [-2, 1]] to get I.
Compute B · A to get I.

slides.altText: Concrete 2×2 example where a candidate B is multiplied with A on both sides to produce the identity matrix I.

slides.title: Continue the example with the system solution
bullets: For any b, the solution of Ax = b is x = A⁻¹b.
Using A⁻¹ = [[1, 0], [-2, 1]], compute x from x = A⁻¹b.
slides.speakerNotes: Pick one specific b if you want to show one numerical solve, but keep focus on the formula x = A⁻¹b and the fact that the inverse lets you solve uniquely for every b.

slides.title: Product inverses reverse the order
bullets: If A and B are invertible, then (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹.
You reverse order because composing AB then undoing it must undo B first.
The formula only applies when both inverses exist.
slides.speakerNotes: Give the key identity and tie it to the idea of undoing operations. The goal is to prevent the common mistake of keeping the same order.
slides.altText: Identity (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹ shown with arrows indicating order reversal.

slides.title: Why order matters in matrix multiplication
bullets: Matrix multiplication is defined by row–column dot products.
Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative, so AB can differ from BA.
Matrix multiplication can be associative and distributes over addition.
slides.speakerNotes: Reground the inverse-of-a-product rule in the fact that multiplication order matters. Associativity/distributivity justify algebraic manipulation as long as factor order is preserved.
slides.altText: Row of A dotted with column of B gives entries of AB, with AB vs BA potentially different but multiplication still associative.

slides.title: Invertibility fails when columns are dependent
bullets: A square matrix can fail to be invertible when its columns are linearly dependent.
Linearly dependent columns mean A does not have n pivots.
So a determinant of 0 corresponds to no inverse.
slides.speakerNotes: State the columns-dependent reason for failure of invertibility, and link it back to the pivot and determinant criteria from earlier slides.
slides.altText: A 3×3-like picture where dependent columns prevent reaching n pivots, leading to determinant 0 and no inverse.

slides.title: Misconception checks (nonzero does not mean invertible)
bullets: Misconception: Every nonzero matrix has an inverse.
Correction: A square matrix with determinant 0 can be nonzero yet have no inverse, such as one with two equal rows.
Another misconception: (AB)⁻¹ = A⁻¹B⁻¹.
slides.speakerNotes: Address the two named misconceptions directly so students can actively correct their intuition before homework.
slides.altText: Two side-by-side misconception tiles: nonzero implies inverse (incorrect), and keeping order in (AB)⁻¹ = A⁻¹B⁻¹ (incorrect).

slides.title: Misconception checks (order reversal)
bullets: Correction for the product: (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹ when both inverses exist.
If you want to undo AB, you must undo B before undoing A.

body.markdown:
## Week 5 Study Guide: Determinants and their properties

### Key terms (what you should mean)
- **Determinant (det(A))**: a **scalar** computed from a **square matrix**. **Nonzero exactly when** the matrix is **invertible**. Geometrically, **|det(A)| scales area/volume** under the transformation.
- **Invertible matrix**: an n×n matrix A with a matrix B such that **AB = BA = I**. Equivalently: **det(A) ≠ 0**.
- **Multiplicative property**: **det(AB) = det(A)det(B)**.
- **Row-operation effects on det** (predictable changes):
  - swapping two rows **flips the sign** of the determinant
  - scaling one row by c **multiplies det by c**
  - adding a multiple of one row to another **does not change det**

### Misconceptions to watch for (and how to correct them)
1) **“det(A + B) = det(A) + det(B)”** → Wrong: the determinant is **multiplicative, not additive**. You should use **det(AB)=det(A)det(B)**; **det(A+B) usually differs** from det(A)+det(B).
2) **“Small entries means small determinant / large determinant means a big matrix”** → Wrong: determinant measures **invertibility and volume scaling**, not entry size. A matrix can have **large numbers yet det = 0**.
3) **“Vectors are always arrows in 2D or 3D space.”** → Wrong: anything satisfying vector-space axioms is a vector: **polynomials, matrices, and functions** are included.
4) **“Any subset of R^n is a vector space.”** → Wrong: a subset must contain the **zero vector** and be **closed** under addition and scalar multiplication.
5) **“Every nonzero matrix has an inverse.”** → Wrong: a square matrix can be **nonzero but singular** (e.g., two equal rows) so **det = 0** and there is **no inverse**.
6) **“(AB)⁻¹ = A⁻¹B⁻¹.”** → Wrong: order reverses: **(AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹**.

### Self-check prompts
- If det(A)=0, what can you conclude about invertibility—and what does that imply about whether Ax=b has a **unique** solution for every b?
- If you swap two rows of A, how does det(A) change?
- Which is reliable: det(AB)=det(A)det(B) or det(A+B)=det(A)+det(B)?

### If you missed the reading
Revisit the idea that the determinant is a **single number computed from a square matrix** that is **nonzero exactly when the matrix is invertible**. Use **|det(A)|** to remember the determinant’s geometric role: it **scales area/volume** under the transformation. Then anchor your work on the two big algebra facts you’ll reuse constantly: **det(AB)=det(A)det(B)** and the **row-operation rules** (swap flips sign, scale multiplies, add-multiple leaves det unchanged). Finally, don’t confuse determinant behavior with **entry size**—large entries do not guarantee a nonzero determinant.

## Week 6 Study Guide: Vector Spaces and Subspaces

### Key terms (what you must be able to use)
- **Vector space**: A set of objects with **addition** and **scalar multiplication** that satisfy the vector-space axioms (closure, associativity, commutativity, identity element, inverses, distributivity). **A vector space must contain the zero vector, and every vector must have an additive inverse.**
- **Subspace**: A subset of a vector space that **(1) contains the zero vector** and is **(2) closed under addition and (3) closed under scalar multiplication.**
- **Span**: For vectors S, **span(S)** is the set of **all linear combinations** of vectors in S. **The span of a set of vectors is always a subspace**, and it is the **smallest** subspace containing S.

### Misconceptions to watch for
- “**Vectors are always arrows in 2D or 3D space.**” — False. **Anything satisfying the vector-space axioms is a vector—polynomials, matrices, and functions included; geometry is one model, not the definition.**
- “**Any subset of R^n is a vector space.**” — False. You still need **zero vector** and **closure** under addition + scalar multiplication. **A line not through the origin fails all three.**
- “**Any line or plane in R^3 is a subspace.**” — False. **Only lines and planes through the origin are subspaces; others miss the zero vector and are not closed under scaling.**
- “**The span of two vectors is always a plane.**” — False. If the two vectors are **parallel (or one is zero), their span collapses to a line or a point**; the span’s dimension depends on independence.

### Self-check prompts (answer without looking)
1. If a subset contains two vectors but does **not** contain the zero vector, can it be a subspace? Why?
2. Take two vectors that point in the same direction. What does their **span** look like?
3. Give one non-geometric example of a vector space (not arrows).

### If you missed the reading
A **vector space** is defined by the operations and the axioms, not by geometry. A **subspace** is stricter: it must be a subset that contains the **zero vector** and is closed under **addition** and **scalar multiplication**. If you’re asked about a **line/plane**, quickly check whether it passes through the origin and whether scaling stays in the set. When you hear **span**, remember it means **all linear combinations**, and it is always a subspace—also the smallest one containing the vectors.

body.a: No. If an object collection has addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the vector-space axioms, then its elements are vectors, even if they are polynomials, matrices, or functions.

body.a: No. A subset must contain the zero vector and be closed under addition and scalar multiplication; otherwise it fails the vector-space (or subspace) requirements.

body.text: Kickoff for Week 7: distinguish three linked ideas—linear independence (no nontrivial dependence), basis (independent + spans), and dimension (size of any basis). Emphasize: independence is about “redundancy,” not whether vectors look different.

Worked example: Determine whether {(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)} is linearly independent. Set up a linear combination a(1,0)+b(0,1)+c(1,1)=(0,0). This gives equations a+c=0 and b+c=0. Choose c=1, then a=-1 and b=-1 to get a nontrivial solution, so the set is dependent. Connect directly to the misconception: distinct vectors can still be dependent.

Independence-to-basis mini-lab (small groups): For each candidate set, decide if it is independent, spans, both, or neither. Then identify the implied coordinates/dimension when the set is a basis. Target checks: (i) zero vector forces dependence, (ii) dimension counts basis vectors, not all vectors in the space.

Formal summary + R^n logic: (1) Basis = independent + spans; (2) any basis of a finite-dimensional space has the same number of vectors (that number is dimension); (3) in R^n, any n independent vectors form a basis; any spanning set of n vectors is automatically independent. Tie back to span/subspace language from last week: span(S) is a subspace; dimension links to whether adding vectors increases rank.

Reteach one worked example to lock the reading’s core: use the same set {(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)} and re-check dependence. Start from a(1,0)+b(0,1)+c(1,1)=(0,0) and show the nontrivial dependence explicitly (a=-1, b=-1, c=1). Then convert the lesson into a decision rule: to prove independence you must rule out *every* nontrivial solution; to prove dependence it’s enough to exhibit one nontrivial combination giving the zero vector.

body.markdown:
## Week 7 Study Guide: independence → basis → dimension

### Key definitions (what to write on your scratch paper)
- **Linear independence:** A set of vectors is independent if the only linear combination that equals the **zero vector** uses **all zero coefficients**. If you find a **nontrivial** combination that equals the zero vector, you’ve found a **dependence relation**.
- **Dependence test idea:** A set is dependent **exactly when** some vector in the set is a **linear combination of the others**.
- **Basis:** A set that is **linearly independent** *and* **spans** the vector space. (Both conditions matter.)
- **Dimension:** The common **number of vectors in any basis**. Dimension counts **basis vectors**, not “how many vectors the space has.”
- **Vector space (reminder):** Must satisfy the axioms under addition/scalar multiplication, including having a **zero vector**; it’s not restricted to geometric arrows.
- **Subspace (reminder):** A subset is a subspace if it contains the **zero vector** and is **closed** under addition and scalar multiplication.

### Misconceptions to watch for (read these like alerts)
- **“Independent means the vectors are different from each other.”** Distinct vectors can be dependent—independence is about redundancy.
- **“More vectors give more independence.”** In **R^n**, any set of **more than n** vectors is automatically **dependent**.
- **“A vector space has only one basis.”** There are infinitely many bases; what’s fixed is the **size**.
- **“Dimension is the number of vectors in the space.”** Dimension counts **basis vectors**, not members. (R^2 has infinitely many vectors but dimension 2.)

### Quick self-checks
1) If a set contains the **zero vector**, is it independent? (You should be able to answer immediately.)
2) If a vector space has a basis with 3 vectors, what is its **dimension**? (Not “how many total vectors it has.”)
3) Can a set be **distinct but still dependent**? Give a concrete example.

### If you missed the reading
Think of **linear dependence** as a “redundancy certificate”: if one vector can be rebuilt from the others using coefficients, then the set is dependent. A **basis** is not just a spanning set and not just an independent set—it must do **both**. **Dimension** is the **size of a basis**; different bases can look different and have different vectors, but they all have the same number of vectors.

followUps: If you replace (2,1) with (1,1), does your decision change? Explain using the dependence relation.
How would your reasoning connect to the statement “Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution” when these vectors are viewed as columns of a matrix?
If the three vectors were in R^n for a different n, what would you need to know to decide whether n vectors can form a basis?

Finally, compute the coordinates of a given vector as the unique linear combination of the basis vectors you found.

body.q: If the vectors are all different from one another, are they automatically linearly independent?
body.a: No. Distinct vectors can still be dependent; independence is about redundancy, meaning whether a nontrivial linear combination can produce the zero vector.

body.q: Why can a vector space have more than one basis if each vector has unique coordinates in a basis?
body.a: A space can have infinitely many bases. The uniqueness is only within a chosen basis; what stays fixed for a given space is the number of vectors in any basis, which equals the dimension.

slides.title: Where we are in the story
bullets: A vector space comes with addition and scalar multiplication that satisfy the vector-space axioms.
Linear independence, basis, and dimension describe how many “directions” are needed to build everything in the space.
slides.speakerNotes: We already set up vector spaces and subspaces; now we measure structure inside them. Independence tells us when vectors are redundant; basis tells us when a set both spans and has no redundancy; dimension tells us how many vectors a basis must have.
slides.altText: A roadmap slide: vector spaces lead to linear independence, then to basis, then to dimension.

slides.title: Linear independence: the definition
bullets: Vectors are linearly independent when the only linear combination equal to the zero vector uses all zero coefficients.
A nontrivial linear combination that equals the zero vector is a dependence relation.
slides.speakerNotes: Emphasize the “only” and the “zero vector.” If there exists coefficients not all zero that sum to zero, independence fails immediately.
slides.altText: Two sentences: independence means only the trivial combination gives the zero vector.

slides.title: Fast independence checks
bullets: A set containing the zero vector is automatically linearly dependent.
A set of vectors is dependent exactly when some vector in it is a linear combination of the others.
slides.speakerNotes: These give quick shortcuts without solving for everything from scratch. For dependence, it is enough to find one vector that can be rebuilt from the others.
slides.altText: Checklist: zero vector implies dependent; dependence means one vector equals a combination of the rest.

slides.title: Matrix viewpoint: columns of A
bullets: The columns of a matrix A are independent exactly when Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution.
When Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution, every column is a pivot column.
slides.speakerNotes: Connect independence to solving a homogeneous system. Students often think “independence” is geometric; here it is algebraic through Ax = 0.
slides.altText: A matrix A with its columns labeled as pivot columns when Ax equals zero has only the trivial solution.

slides.title: Worked example of independence vs dependence
bullets: Even though v1, v2, and v3 are pairwise different, they are dependent because v3 = v1 + v2.
slides.speakerNotes: Write the dependence relation explicitly: (1, 1) − (1, 0) − (0, 1) = (0, 0). This is a nontrivial combination equal to the zero vector, so the set is not independent.
slides.altText: Three vectors in R^2 showing the dependence relation v3 = v1 + v2.

slides.title: Basis: independence + spanning
bullets: A basis is a linearly independent set that spans the space.
Every basis of a given space has the same number of vectors, and that number is the space’s dimension.
slides.speakerNotes: Keep the two conditions distinct: independent prevents redundancy, and spanning ensures you can build every vector in the space. Dimension then follows as the shared size of any basis.
slides.altText: A basis as a set that is both independent and spanning, with dimension counting basis vectors.

slides.title: Coordinates and unique representation
bullets: Every vector in the space is a unique linear combination of basis vectors.
The coefficients in that unique combination are the vector’s coordinates in that basis.
slides.speakerNotes: This uniqueness is a direct consequence of having a basis. Students should see coordinates as the bookkeeping that turns vectors into numbers.
slides.altText: A vector decomposed uniquely into a sum of basis vectors with listed coefficients.

slides.title: Dimension: what it counts (and what it does not)
bullets: Dimension is the number of vectors in any basis, not the total number of vectors in the space.
In R^n, any n independent vectors form a basis, and any spanning set of n vectors is automatically independent.
slides.speakerNotes: Tie dimension to basis size. Also highlight the R^n shortcut: n vectors are enough to be a basis if they are independent (or enough if they span).
slides.altText: A note: dimension counts basis vectors; in R^n, n independent vectors make a basis.

slides.title: Common misconceptions to avoid
bullets: Independence is not the same as “being different vectors.”
A vector space has infinitely many bases; only the size of a basis is fixed.
slides.speakerNotes: Reinforce the two big error patterns: distinctness does not guarantee independence, and uniqueness of the basis is wrong—only dimension is fixed. Independence concerns redundancy.
slides.altText: Two warning icons: distinctness ≠ independence; only basis size is fixed.

slides.title: Closing the loop: independence → basis → dimension
bullets: To build a basis, you need a set that is both linearly independent and spanning.
To get the dimension, count how many vectors any basis has.
slides.speakerNotes: End by summarizing the logical chain. If you can identify a basis, dimension is immediate as its vector count.
slides.altText: A chain diagram: independent + spanning yields basis, and basis size yields dimension.

body.markdown:
## Week 8 Midterm Study Guide (Systems → Subspaces)

### Core definitions / rules you must use
- **Subspace**: A subset of a vector space that **contains the zero vector** and is **closed under addition** and **scalar multiplication**. Also, the **span** of vectors (all linear combinations) is **always** a subspace. The span is the **smallest** subspace containing the given vectors.
- **System solutions**: A linear system has **exactly zero, one, or infinitely many solutions**.
  - **Consistent** = at least one solution.
  - **Inconsistent** = no solutions.
- **Consistency example template**: If you see equations like **x + y = 1** and **x + y = 3**, they represent **parallel lines that never meet**, so the system is **inconsistent** (0 solutions).
- **Row reduction**:
  - Elementary row operations are **reversible** and **preserve the solution set**.
  - **Pivot positions** are determined by the **echelon structure** during elimination, not by the **size** of entries.
  - Reduced row echelon form is unique (even if you take different elimination paths).
- **Vectors / vector spaces**:
  - Anything satisfying the vector-space axioms is a vector **(polynomials, matrices, functions included)**; geometry is a model, not the definition.
  - A subset is a vector space iff it has the **zero vector** and is **closed** under the operations.

### Misconceptions to watch for (these cost points)
- “**Any line or plane in R^3 is a subspace**.” → Wrong unless it **passes through the origin**.
- “**The span of two vectors is always a plane**.” → If vectors are **parallel (or one is zero)**, span collapses to a **line (or point)**; dimension depends on independence.
- “**Every system of equations has a solution**.” → Not true; parallel inconsistent equations give **0 solutions**.
- “If a system has more than one solution, it has **some finite** number of solutions.” → Over the reals: **two distinct solutions ⇒ infinitely many**.

### Self-check prompts
1) For a proposed subset S, can you explicitly verify: **(i) 0 ∈ S**, **(ii) u,v∈S ⇒ u+v∈S**, **(iii) u∈S, c scalar ⇒ cu∈S**?
2) When you see two different solutions in a linear system over the reals, what must the solution set look like: **exactly two, or infinitely many**?
3) When choosing pivots, are you looking at **largest entries**, or the **first nonzero entry / echelon structure**?

### If you missed the reading
If you only remember “solve the system,” you should also remember what the system can do: it must have **0, 1, or infinitely many** solutions—never exactly two. For subspaces, don’t rely on geometry; use the definition: **contains the zero vector + closed under addition and scalar multiplication**. When using row reduction, elimination is valid because row operations are **reversible** and **preserve the solution set**; pivots come from the echelon form structure, not from entry magnitude.

slides.title: Week 8, Session 1: Midterm exam
bullets: This midterm covers systems of linear equations through subspaces.
You will move between augmented matrices, solution sets, spans, column spaces, and null spaces.
slides.speakerNotes: Today is the exam day, so the goal of the slide deck is to remind you what you must be able to do. The most common grading issues are consistency (none/one/infinite), subspace conditions (zero vector and closure), and confusing span with geometric dimension.
slides.altText: Midterm exam reminder: systems of linear equations through subspaces.

slides.title: Systems: what counts as a solution
bullets: A solution assigns values to every variable so that every equation holds simultaneously.
A linear system has exactly zero, one, or infinitely many solutions, and it never has exactly two.
slides.speakerNotes: When you check work, you should be able to say exactly how many solutions there are and justify it from the matrix form or the equations.
slides.altText: Solutions satisfy all equations; solution counts are zero, one, or infinitely many.

slides.title: Consistency vs inconsistency
bullets: A system is consistent when at least one solution exists.
A system is inconsistent when no solution exists.
slides.speakerNotes: In row-reduction terms, inconsistency is recognized when you get a contradiction in the echelon form. Consistent systems are the ones where row reduction lets you read off solutions.
slides.altText: Consistent means at least one solution; inconsistent means no solutions.

slides.title: Represent systems using augmented matrices
bullets: Every linear system can be represented compactly as an augmented matrix.
You solve the augmented matrix by row reduction.
slides.speakerNotes: Your workflow on the exam should be systematic: translate equations to an augmented matrix, row-reduce, then interpret the reduced echelon form to describe the solution set.
slides.altText: Augmented matrices represent systems, and you solve by row reduction.

slides.title: Row reduction preserves the solution set
bullets: Row reduction uses elementary row operations to reach an echelon form from which solutions can be read off.
Elementary row operations do not change the solution set of the linear system the matrix represents.
slides.speakerNotes: Reversibility of row operations is the key idea: they are designed so that the same solutions are obtained. So if your final answer changes because of row operations, you have made an arithmetic or logic mistake.
slides.altText: Elementary row operations preserve solutions and lead to echelon form.

slides.title: Pivots and free variables
bullets: A pivot is the first nonzero entry of a row in echelon form.
Pivot positions determine which variables are basic and which are free.
slides.speakerNotes: This connects directly to whether you get a unique solution or infinitely many solutions. If there is at least one free variable, you will have infinitely many solutions.
slides.altText: Pivot positions determine basic versus free variables.

slides.title: Concrete worked example: two distinct solutions imply infinitely many
bullets: Consider the system x + y = 1 and x + y = 3.
This system is inconsistent because the two equations cannot hold simultaneously.
slides.speakerNotes: This example targets the 'two solutions' misconception. Over the real numbers, a linear system can have zero, one, or infinitely many solutions, so you should never try to force a finite count like two.
slides.altText: Example of inconsistent system: x + y = 1 and x + y = 3.

slides.title: Another key worked example: span leads to subspaces
bullets: The span of a set of vectors is the set of all their linear combinations.
The span of any set of vectors is always a subspace.
slides.speakerNotes: This matters because subspaces show up as column spaces and null spaces. On the exam, you may be asked to recognize what subspace a given set actually describes via spans.
slides.altText: Span is all linear combinations and is always a subspace.

slides.title: Subspace test: zero vector and closure
bullets: A subspace contains the zero vector.
A subspace is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
slides.speakerNotes: If a candidate set misses the zero vector, it fails immediately. If closure fails (adding two members or scaling a member can leave the set), it also fails immediately.
slides.altText: Subspaces contain zero and are closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

slides.title: Common misconception 1: lines and planes are not automatically subspaces
bullets: Only lines and planes through the origin are subspaces.
A line or plane not through the origin misses the zero vector and is not closed under scaling.
slides.speakerNotes: Use the zero vector test first. If the set does not include the origin, it cannot be a subspace no matter how it looks geometrically.
slides.altText: Lines or planes through the origin can be subspaces; others cannot.

slides.title: Common misconception 2: span of two vectors is not always a plane
bullets: If two vectors are parallel (or one is zero), their span collapses to a line or a point.
The span's dimension depends on whether the vectors are linearly independent.
slides.speakerNotes: You do not get to assume 'two vectors means a plane.' Independence controls what the span actually looks like, and on the exam you should justify it using the linear combinations viewpoint.
slides.altText: Span of two vectors can be a line or point if vectors are parallel or dependent.

slides.title: Column space and consistency of Ax = b
bullets: The column space of a matrix A is the span of its columns.
The column space consists exactly of those b for which Ax = b is consistent.
slides.speakerNotes: If you can compute or describe the column space, you can immediately answer which right-hand sides are solvable. This is a subspace viewpoint of consistency.
slides.altText: Column space equals the set of right-hand sides that make Ax = b consistent.

slides.title: Null space and solutions of Ax = 0
bullets: The null space of A is the set of solutions of Ax = 0.
The null space is a subspace of the domain.
slides.speakerNotes: When asked about null space, you should focus on Ax = 0 solutions. The subspace property comes from closure under addition and scalar multiplication of solution sets.
slides.altText: Null space is the solution set of Ax = 0 and forms a subspace.

body.text: Hook + definitions: We connect the three ideas: (1) column space = all outputs Ax can produce, so it’s the span of A’s columns; (2) null space = all inputs that produce zero, so it’s the solution set of Ax = 0; (3) rank = dimension of the column space (number of pivot columns). Emphasize what “consistent” means for Ax = b: b is in the column space exactly when Ax = b has a solution.

Worked example: Column space + consistency check. Take A = [[1,0],[0,1],[0,0]] (so columns are c1 = (1,0,0), c2 = (0,1,0)). Then Ax = x1*c1 + x2*c2, so Ax always lands in the set of vectors (y1,y2,0). That means the column space is span{(1,0,0),(0,1,0)} = {(y1,y2,0)}. Now test b = (2,3,0): since z=0, Ax=b is consistent. Test b = (2,3,4): impossible because every Ax has third component 0, so Ax=b is inconsistent and b is not in the column space.

Quick group practice: Students compute which vectors belong to column space and null space using “Ax must match the patterns.” Then they answer: what is rank(A)? Use the idea that rank is the dimension of the column space (pivot columns). Wrap with: for an m-by-n matrix, rank + nullity = n.

Reteach worked example (same one as above): We revisit the pattern reasoning from A = [[1,0],[0,1],[0,0]]. Explain again: Ax = x1(1,0,0) + x2(0,1,0) = (x1,x2,0). Core correction: If you’re thinking “any plane/line is a subspace,” stop—here the column space is exactly those vectors with third coordinate 0 because it must contain 0 and be closed under scaling. Then revisit consistency: Ax=b is consistent iff b has form (y1,y2,0). Finally, connect rank: the column space is 2-dimensional (two independent columns), so rank(A)=2.

Systems + rank sanity checks: connect rank-nullity to “solutions exist” logic. Reinforce that linear systems have either zero, one, or infinitely many solutions—never exactly two. Also warn about rank misconceptions: rank counts pivots after row reduction; rank never exceeds the smaller of row/column counts because dependence reduces it.

## Week 9 Study Guide: Column space, null space, rank

**Key terms (what you should be able to say in one sentence each)**
- **Subspace**: a subset of a vector space that **contains the zero vector** and is **closed under addition and scalar multiplication**. The **span** of a set of vectors (all linear combinations) is always a subspace.
- **Column space Col(A)**: the **span of the columns** of A; it is **exactly the set of b for which Ax = b is consistent**.
- **Null space Nul(A)**: the set of **solutions to Ax = 0**; it is a subspace of the domain.
- **Rank**: the **dimension of the column space** (equivalently, the number of pivot columns). **Rank(A) + nullity(A) = n** for an m-by-n matrix.

**Misconceptions to watch for (you will be tested on these)**
1. “**Any line or plane in R^3 is a subspace.**” Remember: **Only lines and planes through the origin are subspaces; others miss the zero vector and are not closed under scaling.**
2. “**The span of two vectors is always a plane.**” Remember: **If the two vectors are parallel (or one is zero), their span collapses to a line or a point; the span's dimension depends on independence.**
3. “**Rank is the number of nonzero entries or nonzero rows in the original matrix.**” Remember: **Rank counts pivots AFTER row reduction; a matrix full of nonzero entries can still have rank 1 if its rows are proportional.**
4. “**A tall matrix with many rows has large rank.**” Remember: **Rank never exceeds the smaller of the row and column counts, and dependence among columns lowers it further.**
5. Systems of equations: **zero, one, or infinitely many solutions—never exactly two.** Also, two distinct real solutions imply infinitely many.

**Self-check prompts (do these without looking)**
- If **b is in the column space of A**, what does that guarantee about the system **Ax=b**?
- If **v is in the null space**, what equation must it satisfy (write it exactly)?
- For an m-by-n matrix, if **rank(A)=r**, what is **rank(A)+nullity(A)**?

### If you missed the reading
Start by forcing the definitions to be operational: **Col(A)** is “all outputs Ax can produce,” and **Nul(A)** is “all inputs that make Ax=0.” Then practice the consistency test: **b ∈ Col(A)** exactly when **Ax=b** has at least one solution. Finally, remember rank is a **dimension/pivot count** idea, not a “number of nonzeros” idea—row reduction reveals pivots, and dependencies reduce rank.

## Week 10 Study Guide: Linear transformations and their matrices

### Core ideas to remember
- **Linear system (solution counting + consistency):** A linear system has **exactly zero, one, or infinitely many solutions** (never exactly two). It’s **consistent** if **at least one solution exists** and **inconsistent** if **no solution exists**. Also, every linear system can be represented as an **augmented matrix** and solved by **row reduction**.
- **Linear transformations → matrices:** A matrix can represent a linear transformation so you can compute outputs systematically from inputs.
- **Matrix operations (two different “multiplications”):**
  - **Addition and scalar multiplication** act **entrywise**.
  - **Matrix product AB** is defined only when the number of columns of **A equals the number of rows of B**.
  - The **(i,j) entry of AB** is the **dot product** of **row i of A** with **column j of B**.
- **Matrix multiplication is not commutative:** In general **AB ≠ BA**, and one of the products may not even be defined.
- **Vector spaces (what “vectors” really are):** A vector space is a set closed under addition and scalar multiplication that satisfies the axioms (including **zero vector** and **additive inverses**). Examples: **polynomials, matrices, and functions**—geometry is one model, not the definition.

### Misconceptions to watch for (and how to correct them)
1. **“Every system of equations has a solution.”** Correction: **A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet.**
2. **“If a system has more than one solution, then it has finitely many.”** Correction: **Over the real numbers, once a linear system has two distinct solutions it has infinitely many, because the whole line through the two solutions solves the system.**
3. **“Matrix multiplication works entrywise, like addition.”** Correction: **The product AB combines rows of A with columns of B via dot products; the entrywise product is a different, rarely used operation.**
4. **“AB = BA for matrices, as with numbers.”** Correction: **Order matters in matrix products; AB = BA only in special cases, such as when one factor is the identity or both are powers of the same matrix.**
5. **“Vectors are always arrows in 2D or 3D space.”** Correction: **Anything satisfying the vector-space axioms is a vector — polynomials, matrices, and functions included; geometry is one model, not the definition.**
6. **“Any subset of R^n is a vector space.”** Correction: **A subset must contain the zero vector and be closed under addition and scalar multiplication; a line not through the origin fails all three.**

### Self-check prompts
- If you see **x + y = 1** and **x + y = 3**, what does “inconsistent” mean, and how many solutions are there?
- For matrices, what does the **(i,j) entry of AB** compute—entrywise multiplication, or a dot product of a row with a column?
- Pick the correct statement: does **AB = BA** always hold? If not, under what special cases can it?

### If you missed the reading
Linear systems are categorized by how many solutions they have: **zero, one, or infinitely many**. Consistency means at least one solution exists, and inconsistency means none exists. For matrices, remember that **AB is defined via row–column dot products** (not entrywise multiplication), and **order matters** in matrix products. Finally, “vector” means anything that satisfies the **vector-space axioms**—not just geometric arrows.

body.markdown:
## Week 11 Study Guide: Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors (plus key algebra facts)

### Core definitions (use these every time)
- **Eigenvector / eigenvalue:** For a square matrix **A**, a **nonzero** vector **x** is an eigenvector if **Ax = λx**. The scalar **λ** is the **eigenvalue**.
- **Finding eigenvalues:** Solve **det(A − λI) = 0** (so λ is a root of the characteristic polynomial).
- **Finding eigenvectors:** For each eigenvalue λ, solve **(A − λI)x = 0** and then take **nonzero** solutions.
- **Diagonalizable criterion (from this unit’s kernel fact):** An **n×n** matrix is diagonalizable **exactly when** it has **n linearly independent eigenvectors**.
- **Independence:** Eigenvectors from **distinct eigenvalues** are **automatically linearly independent**.

### Key “don’t mess this up” misconceptions to watch
1) **Zero vector as an eigenvector**
   - Wrong belief (in students’ own words): “**The zero vector is an eigenvector for every eigenvalue.**”
   - Repair: **Eigenvectors are required to be nonzero — A0 = λ0 holds trivially and identifies nothing about the matrix.**

2) **Zero eigenvalue implies zero matrix**
   - Wrong belief: “**A matrix with a zero eigenvalue is a zero matrix.**”
   - Repair: **A zero eigenvalue only means some nonzero vector is sent to zero — the matrix is singular, not necessarily zero.**

3) **Matrix multiplication as entrywise multiplication**
   - Wrong belief: “**Matrix multiplication works entrywise, like addition.**”
   - Repair: **The product AB combines rows of A with columns of B via dot products; the entrywise product is a different, rarely used operation.**

4) **Commuting multiplication**
   - Wrong belief: “**AB = BA for matrices, as with numbers.**”
   - Repair: **Order matters in matrix products; AB = BA only in special cases, such as when one factor is the identity or both are powers of the same matrix.**

5) **Vectors are only geometric arrows**
   - Wrong belief: “**Vectors are always arrows in 2D or 3D space.**”
   - Repair: **Anything satisfying the vector-space axioms is a vector — polynomials, matrices, and functions included; geometry is one model, not the definition.**

6) **Any subset of R^n is a vector space**
   - Wrong belief: “**Any subset of R^n is a vector space.**”
   - Repair: **A subset must contain the zero vector and be closed under addition and scalar multiplication; a line not through the origin fails all three.**

### Self-check prompts (quick)
- If you claim **Ax = λx**, what two things must be checked? (Look back: nonzero x + scalar multiple relationship.)
- If **λ = 0** is an eigenvalue, what does that tell you about **invertibility** and about **Ax** for some nonzero x?
- When computing **(AB)_{ij}**, which parts of A and B are involved in that dot product? (Row i of A with column j of B.)

### If you missed the reading
The key workflow is: **eigenvalues come from det(A − λI) = 0**, then **eigenvectors come from solving (A − λI)x = 0**. Remember: **eigenvectors must be nonzero**, even though **A0 = λ0** is always true and doesn’t tell you anything. Also, a **zero eigenvalue** means **some nonzero vector is mapped to zero** (so A is **singular**), not that **A must be the zero matrix**. Finally, keep matrix multiplication straight: **AB uses dot products of rows with columns**, and **order matters**.

body.markdown:
## Diagonalization: the parts you must not mix up

**Eigenvector test:** For a square matrix **A**, a vector **x** is an eigenvector only if **x is nonzero** and **Ax = λx**. The eigenvalue **λ** is found from the characteristic polynomial: **det(A − λI) = 0**.

**Zero eigenvalue vs zero matrix:** A **zero eigenvalue** means **some nonzero vector** gets sent to zero: **Ax = 0** for at least one **x ≠ 0**. That tells you **A is not invertible (singular)**, but **A need not be the zero matrix**.

**Diagonalizable criterion:** An **n-by-n** matrix is **diagonalizable exactly when it has n linearly independent eigenvectors**.

**Distinct eigenvalues help:** Eigenvectors from **distinct eigenvalues are automatically linearly independent**, which makes the “count to n” step easier.

### Misconceptions to watch for
- **“The zero vector is an eigenvector for every eigenvalue.”** (Wrong: eigenvectors are required to be **nonzero**; **A0 = λ0** holds trivially and tells you nothing.)
- **“A matrix with a zero eigenvalue is a zero matrix.”** (Wrong: λ = 0 only means **some nonzero vector is sent to zero**; the matrix is **singular**, not necessarily the zero matrix.)

### Self-check prompts
1) If you solve (A − λI)x = 0 and the solution includes x = 0, what tells you the eigenvector condition is satisfied? (Answer: you must choose a **nonzero** solution.)
2) If λ = 0 is an eigenvalue, does that force A to be the zero matrix? Why or why not? (Answer: no—only guarantees singularity because a **nonzero** vector maps to 0.)
3) To decide diagonalizable, what exact number are you trying to reach, and what property must the eigenvectors have? (Answer: **n linearly independent eigenvectors**.)

### If you missed the reading
Diagonalization relies on the eigenvector equation **Ax = λx** with **x nonzero**, and the eigenvalues come from **det(A − λI) = 0**. A matrix is diagonalizable exactly when you can find **n linearly independent eigenvectors**. Do not confuse “λ = 0 exists” with “A is the zero matrix”—λ = 0 only means some **nonzero** vector gets sent to **0**, making A singular.
