body.text: Set the stage: orthogonality, projections, and least squares as one workflow. Start from the definition-level facts: orthogonality means inner product 0; projection is a linear map P with P^2=P; least squares is “project b onto the column space of A,” equivalently minimizing the residual length. Emphasize the geometry is a consequence, not the definition.

Mini-worked example (conceptual): Take a vector b and a subspace W (think: a column space). Describe projecting b onto W: the projected vector is the closest point in W to b, and the residual b − proj_W(b) is orthogonal to W. Then connect to least squares: solving Ax̂≈b means Ax̂ is that projection of b onto Im(A). Walk the logic chain explicitly: closest point ⇔ residual orthogonal ⇔ normal equations (A^T A x̂ = A^T b).

Guided checks + misconception traps. Students answer short multiple-choice prompts focusing on statements that sound right but fail: (1) “orthogonal just means perpendicular lines in a picture,” (2) “projection changes the subspace you project onto,” (3) “if P is a projection then Im(P) ⟂ Ker(P) always,” (4) “least squares finds an exact solution,” and (5) “best-fit line must pass through data points.” For each wrong pick, students justify using one kernel fact (definition or theorem statement).

Reteach with the same mini-worked example described earlier (the “project b onto the column space of A” example). Re-walk it but slower: (i) orthogonality is defined by inner product 0 (works even when there’s no picture), (ii) the projection Px maps points into the subspace and leaves vectors already in the subspace unchanged, (iii) in the orthogonal projection case the residual is perpendicular to the subspace, and (iv) least squares chooses x̂ so that Ax̂ is the closest point in Im(A), so Ax̂ generally differs from b. End with the normal-equations connection to lock the computational meaning.

Wrap with transfer: connect projection tests (P^2=P; orthogonal iff also P^T=P in the real case) and system-solution structure (exactly zero/one/infinitely many). Reinforce why least squares belongs to inconsistent systems (no exact solution) and how orthogonality underlies the optimal approximation.

body.markdown:
## Week 13 Study Guide (Orthogonality → Projections → Least Squares)

### Core definitions & facts to know
- **Orthogonality:** Two vectors are orthogonal when their **dot product / inner product is 0**. This definition extends beyond pictures to **functions and high-dimensional data**.
- **Projection operator:** A linear map **P is a projection iff P² = P**. For any vector v, relative to the projection you can decompose **v = Pv + (v − Pv)** with **Pv ∈ Im(P)** and **v − Pv ∈ Ker(P)**.
- **Orthogonal vs oblique projection:** For an **orthogonal projection**, we have **Ker(P) = (Im(P))^⊥** and **Im(P) = (Ker(P))^⊥**. In the real case, **orthogonal projection ⇔ P^T = P and P² = P**. If P is merely a projection with **P^T ≠ P**, the perpendicular relationship between Im(P) and Ker(P) may fail.
- **Least squares:** The least-squares solution **x̂** of an inconsistent system **Ax = b** minimizes the **length of the residual** **b − Ax**. It corresponds to projecting **b onto the column space of A**, and satisfies the **normal equations** **AᵀA x̂ = Aᵀb**.

### Misconceptions to watch for (common traps)
- “Orthogonal just means perpendicular lines in a picture.” (Orthogonality is defined by **inner product = 0**, not by drawing.)
- “Projection changes the subspace you project onto.” (Projection maps points **INTO** the subspace; vectors already in it are unchanged.)
- “If P is a projection, then Im(P) is always perpendicular to Ker(P).” (That perpendicular relationship is guaranteed only for **orthogonal** projections.)
- “Least squares finds an exact solution to the system.” (It minimizes the residual; fitted values **generally differ from b**.)
- “A best-fit line must pass through the data points.” (Least squares minimizes squared vertical gaps and can miss every point.)

### Self-check prompts
1. If I know **P² = P** but not whether **P^T = P**, what perpendicular conclusion (if any) can I safely make about **Im(P)** and **Ker(P)**?
2. Given an inconsistent **Ax = b**, what does **least squares** optimize: making **Ax̂ equal to b**, or making the **residual b − Ax̂** as small as possible (in length)?
3. If **b is projected onto Im(A)**, which vector is orthogonal to the subspace: **Ax̂** or **b − Ax̂**?

### If you missed the reading
Least squares is not “solving exactly when exact solving is impossible.” It is the method that chooses **x̂ so that Ax̂ is the closest point to b inside the column space of A**. That “closest point” idea is tied to **orthogonality**: for an orthogonal projection, the residual **b − Ax̂** is orthogonal to the subspace you projected onto. Finally, don’t assume pictures: orthogonality is defined by the **inner product being zero**, and it extends to vectors like functions and high-dimensional data.

body.prompt: In a least-squares problem, what does “best” mean in terms of the residual b − Ax̂, and how is that related to an orthogonal projection onto the column space of A?
body.tension: Students often assume least squares produces an exact solution or that best-fit objects must pass through the given data, but the geometry says the fit is only the closest point in a column space.
followUps: If you knew Ax̂ is the orthogonal projection of b onto Col(A), what can you say about the residual’s relationship to Col(A)?
How would your answer change if the projection were not orthogonal?
Can you state what condition guarantees uniqueness of the least-squares solution in terms of A’s columns?

body.task: You will analyze projections and connect them to least squares. First, choose a subspace W and a vector v, then compute the orthogonal projection of v onto W using a dot-product formula for your chosen case. Next, reinterpret Ax̂ as the orthogonal projection of b onto the column space of A and explain why the fitted values generally do not equal b in inconsistent systems. Finally, state the normal equations and the uniqueness condition in terms of whether A’s columns are linearly independent.
steps: Pick a concrete W and v in R^2 or R^3 and compute the orthogonal projection p of v onto W and the residual r = v − p.
Verify orthogonality by checking that r has dot product zero with a spanning vector for W.
Let A have columns spanning the column space you are projecting onto, and explain how x̂ makes Ax̂ the orthogonal projection of b onto Col(A).
Write the normal equations A^T A x̂ = A^T b and state when the least-squares solution is unique.

rubricBands.observableBehavior: Student correctly computes an orthogonal projection and checks the residual’s orthogonality to the subspace using dot products.

rubricBands.band: Connect projection geometry to least squares
rubricBands.observableBehavior: Student correctly describes least squares as minimizing residual length and as orthogonal projection of b onto Col(A), and ties that to why Ax̂ typically differs from b.
Student claims least squares finds an exact solution (Ax̂ = b) or claims a best-fit line must pass through all data points.

body.q: Does orthogonal projection always mean perpendicular image and kernel?
body.a: Perpendicular image and kernel is guaranteed for orthogonal projections. For general projections, the perpendicular relationship between Im(P) and Ker(P) need not hold.

body.q: If I use least squares, will the fitted model satisfy the original equations exactly?
body.a: Not in general. Least squares minimizes the length of the residual b − Ax, so the fitted values Ax̂ generally differ from b when the system is inconsistent.

slides.title: Where orthogonality helps
bullets: Two vectors are orthogonal exactly when their dot product is zero.
Orthogonal and orthonormal bases make coordinates, projections, and distance computations simple because the basis directions do not interfere.
slides.speakerNotes: Start by anchoring orthogonality in the dot product being zero. Emphasize that this definition works beyond pictures, including in higher-dimensional and function spaces. Then connect orthogonal bases to simpler coordinate and distance calculations.
slides.altText: Two vectors drawn at right angles with a note that orthogonality means dot product 0; then a basis labeled as orthogonal showing directions not interfering.

slides.title: Basic consequences of orthogonality
bullets: Nonzero orthogonal vectors are automatically linearly independent.
Orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace is the closest point in that subspace to the vector.
slides.speakerNotes: Use linear independence as a quick payoff. Then give the geometric meaning of orthogonal projection: closest point, which will be the key to least squares later.
slides.altText: A vector v and a subspace with a point p on the subspace; p is the closest point to v, with an indication of orthogonality to the residual.

slides.title: From subspaces to projections
bullets: A projection is a linear operator P with P^2 = P.
If P is a projection, then v = Pv + (v − Pv) decomposes into an image part and a residual part.
slides.speakerNotes: Define projection algebraically using P^2 = P. Then interpret the decomposition as “one part lies in Im(P)” and “the leftover lies in the complementary part,” preparing for the orthogonal case distinction.
slides.altText: A diagram splitting v into Pv (inside the projected subspace) and v−Pv (the residual), with an arrow showing v = Pv + (v−Pv).

slides.title: Orthogonal vs general projections
bullets: For an orthogonal projection P, Ker(P) = (Im(P))^⊥ and Im(P) = (Ker(P))^⊥.
For a general projection, this perpendicular relationship need not hold.
slides.speakerNotes: State the perpendicular relationship explicitly for orthogonal projections. Then warn that if the projection is not orthogonal, you cannot assume perpendicularity between Im(P) and Ker(P).
slides.altText: A right-angle mark between a subspace and the residual subspace for orthogonal projection, and a contrast showing no right-angle for a non-orthogonal projection.

slides.title: Orthogonal projection test
bullets: In the real case, P is an orthogonal projection exactly when P is symmetric (P^T = P) and P^2 = P.
So checking P^T = P together with idempotence identifies orthogonal projections.
slides.speakerNotes: This slide turns the theory into a practical condition. Symmetry plus P^2=P is the clean test (in the real case) for orthogonal projection.
slides.altText: A checklist labeled P^2=P and P^T=P for determining an orthogonal projection.

slides.title: Concrete example of an orthogonal projection
bullets: Let W be the line spanned by w = [1, 1]^T in R^2.
For v = [2, 0]^T, the orthogonal projection onto W is p = (v·w)/(w·w) w = (2)/(2) [1, 1]^T = [1, 1]^T.
slides.speakerNotes: Compute an actual projection using the closest-point idea and the dot-product formula for projecting onto a 1D subspace. Then the residual r = v − p will be orthogonal to W by construction.
slides.altText: Coordinate axes with line W through the origin along slope 1, point v at (2,0), projected point p at (1,1), and residual r from p to v.

slides.title: Residual orthogonality in the example
bullets: With p = [1, 1]^T, the residual is r = v − p = [1, −1]^T.
The residual is orthogonal to W because r·w = [1, −1]·[1, 1] = 0.
slides.speakerNotes: Tie back to the kernel/image picture for orthogonal projections: the residual lies in the orthogonal complement. This demonstrates the orthogonal projection property directly.
slides.altText: Show residual vector r pointing from p back to v and indicate a right angle to the line W.

slides.title: Least squares as projection
bullets: For an inconsistent system Ax = b, least squares chooses x̂ minimizing the length of the residual b − Ax.
Geometrically, Ax̂ is the orthogonal projection of b onto the column space of A.
slides.speakerNotes: Connect least squares to orthogonal projection immediately. Emphasize that in the inconsistent case, we cannot expect Ax̂ = b, only the closest approximation in the column space.
slides.altText: A plane or line representing Col(A), point b outside it, and a nearest point Ax̂ on Col(A) with a residual drawn to b.

slides.title: Normal equations and uniqueness
bullets: The least-squares solution x̂ satisfies the normal equations A^T A x̂ = A^T b.
When the columns of A are linearly independent, A^T A is invertible and the least-squares solution is unique.
slides.speakerNotes: Give the algebraic characterization via normal equations. Then state the uniqueness condition exactly as given by invertibility when columns are linearly independent.
slides.altText: A matrix A pointing to a vector b, with an arrow to A^T A x̂ = A^T b, and a label 'invertible' when columns are independent.

slides.title: Least squares misconceptions to avoid
bullets: Least squares minimizes the residual, so Ax̂ generally differs from b in inconsistent systems.
The best-fit line from least squares minimizes squared gaps and can miss every single data point.
slides.speakerNotes: Make students commit to the meaning of “best” in least squares: closest residual length (equivalently orthogonal projection), not exact satisfaction of equations. Then address the common “line must pass through points” belief.
slides.altText: A scatter plot with a fitted line that does not pass through every marked point, and a note that residuals are minimized.

body.text: Warm-up diagnostic (no calculators): we’ll rapidly restate the course “decision rules” that drive correct work on the final: (1) linear systems have 0/1/inf solutions, (2) row operations preserve the solution set, (3) pivots come from echelon structure, (4) subspace tests (contains 0, closed under + and scalar mult), (5) invertibility via n pivots / nonzero determinant, (6) rank = dimension of column space and rank + nullity = n, (7) eigenvectors must be nonzero, (8) orthogonality = inner product 0, (9) orthogonal projection vs general projection, (10) least squares minimizes residual and uses normal equations.

Comprehensive review station work (4 stations, quick rotation): Systems & row reduction; Vector spaces/subspaces/independence-basis-dimension; Matrix algebra & determinants/inverses; Orthogonality/projections/least squares. At each station, students do one “new instance” problem rather than copying a worked example, then they check by the allowed substitution logic (e.g., verify AX=b, or verify A P = P constraints like P^2=P).

Worked example walkthrough (Systems → RREF → consistency): Use the given inconsistency template system x + y = 1 and x + y = 3. We build the augmented matrix, row-reduce, and show the contradiction row corresponds to inconsistent equations. Then we connect it to the rule: linear systems have exactly zero, one, or infinitely many solutions—never exactly two.

Reteach the core read: inconsistency vs infinite solutions using that same worked example, step-by-step. We re-walk the template x + y = 1 and x + y = 3: identify that the equations represent parallel lines, then translate that into augmented-matrix row reduction (a row like [0 0 | 2] means no solutions). Finish by asking students to *substitute back into each equation* for any proposed solution attempt, emphasizing the correctness check.

Final-exam style practice: 6 timed multiple-choice questions (our quiz) with justification. Students pick an answer, then write a one-sentence reason referencing the exact rule (e.g., “pivot positions are determined by echelon structure, not by entry size”).

body.prompt: Pick one topic from this week’s review (systems and row reduction, vector spaces and subspaces, rank, invertibility and determinants, eigenvalues/eigenvectors, projections/least squares). Then explain how you would verify your final answer by substituting back into a defining relation or checking against a clear criterion from row reduction or a definition.
body.tension: People often want to memorize patterns, but review questions are designed to test whether you can apply theorems to new instances and then justify and check your results.
followUps: What specific “definition check” would you do at the end of your solution for your chosen topic?
Which step in your process is the one most likely to go wrong under time pressure, and how will you guard against it?
If your row reduction gives an inconsistent system, what conclusion can you state immediately about the existence of solutions?

body.task: Complete a short set of mixed review problems spanning systems of linear equations, row reduction, and at least one conceptual topic (vector spaces/subspaces, independence/basis/dimension, or rank). For every computed answer, include a final check by substituting back into the original defining relations or by verifying the stated criterion (such as consistency from the row-reduced augmented matrix). Keep your work organized so that an instructor can see the intermediate steps that justify your conclusion.
steps: Solve at least one linear system using an augmented matrix and row reduction, and state whether it is consistent or inconsistent.
Compute the relevant structural information for a second problem, such as pivot count, rank, or a basis/spanning set conclusion, depending on the topic you choose.
For each solution, add a final verification step by substituting back into the original equations or checking the defining property you used.

rubricBands.band: Top band: definition + example applied correctly
rubricBands.observableBehavior: The student states the relevant definition or theorem being used and then applies it to a concrete instance. The student includes a substitution-based or criterion-based verification of the final answer.

rubricBands.band: Middle band: procedure with partial justification
rubricBands.observableBehavior: The student performs most computations correctly but justification or the final verification step is missing or incomplete. The reasoning aligns with the right topic but may not clearly connect the definition to the computation.

The student claims that every system has a solution, or that a system can have exactly two solutions. The student also fails to use consistency criteria from row-reduced form when concluding about solution existence.

slides.title: Week 14: what we do today
bullets: This session is a comprehensive review and a final-exam readiness check.
We focus on re-deriving key results and practicing core computations from earlier topics.
We also practice the habit of checking correctness by substituting back into defining relations.
slides.speakerNotes: State the purpose of the week: connect definitions to procedures, and verify results by plugging back. Emphasize that review problems should feel like new instances, not rehearsed copies.
slides.altText: A roadmap showing “Comprehensive review” and “Final exam readiness,” with arrows to re-deriving, core computations, and substitution checks.

slides.title: Review principle: connect theorems to procedures
bullets: A comprehensive review typically includes re-deriving key results and practicing core computations from the course topics covered to date.
A standard review approach verifies understanding by applying theorems to new instances rather than only reproducing worked examples.
For theorem-based computation, correctness is checked by substituting back into defining relations.
slides.speakerNotes: Give one short example idea: after solving Ax=b, substitute the proposed x back to verify every equation holds. Then pivot to the next slide about systems and consistency.
slides.altText: Three stacked cards: re-derive and practice, apply theorems to new instances, and always check by substitution.

slides.title: Systems of linear equations: the solution patterns
bullets: A system of linear equations is a collection of linear equations in the same variables.
A solution assigns values to each variable so that every equation holds simultaneously.
A linear system has exactly zero, one, or infinitely many solutions.
slides.speakerNotes: Clarify: students sometimes expect “two solutions” because of experience with quadratic equations. Reinforce the allowed counts: 0, 1, or infinitely many.
slides.altText: A Venn-style diagram labeled “solutions” with three regions labeled “none,” “one,” and “infinitely many.”

slides.title: Consistency and augmented matrix + row reduction
bullets: A system is consistent when at least one solution exists and inconsistent when no solution exists.
Every linear system can be represented compactly as an augmented matrix and solved by row reduction.
slides.speakerNotes: Tie consistency to what you see in row reduction: you only need the augmented matrix to decide whether solutions exist. Mention that elimination is the systematic procedure.
slides.altText: An augmented matrix transforms into echelon and reduced row echelon form, with “consistent” or “inconsistent” indicated at the end.

slides.title: Row reduction: what operations do (and do not) do
bullets: Row reduction uses elementary row operations: swap, scale a row by a nonzero constant, and add a multiple of one row to another.
Elementary row operations do not change the solution set of the linear system the matrix represents.
Reduced row echelon form is unique, and pivot positions determine basic versus free variables.
slides.speakerNotes: Emphasize reversibility and solution-set preservation. Then connect pivots to what variables are determined.
slides.altText: A sequence of row-operation icons leading to reduced row echelon form with pivot markers.

slides.title: Worked example: solve and check a system
bullets: Consider the system x + y = 3 and x − y = 1.
Adding the equations gives 2x = 4, so x = 2 and then y = 1.
Checking by substitution confirms both equations hold simultaneously.
slides.speakerNotes: Do the explicit substitution: for (x,y)=(2,1), verify x+y=3 and x−y=1. This is the review habit: validate the computed solution against the original equations.
slides.altText: A system of two equations is solved to get x=2, y=1, with substitution checks shown for both equations.

slides.title: Vector spaces and subspaces: the closure tests
bullets: A vector space is a set with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying closure, associativity, commutativity, identity, inverse, and distributivity axioms.
A subspace is a subset that contains the zero vector and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
slides.speakerNotes: Stress that “subset of R^n” is not enough. The checklist is: contains 0 and is closed under addition and scaling.
slides.altText: A checklist labeled “zero vector” and “closed under addition and scalar multiplication,” connected to “subspace.”

slides.title: Span and the spaces associated to a matrix
bullets: The span of a set of vectors is all their linear combinations and is always a subspace.
The column space of a matrix A is the span of its columns and consists of exactly those b for which Ax = b is consistent.
The null space of A is the set of solutions of Ax = 0 and is a subspace of the domain.
slides.speakerNotes: Connect conceptual definitions to computation: column space relates to consistency of Ax=b, and null space relates to solutions of the homogeneous system.
slides.altText: Three boxes labeled span, column space (Ax=b consistency), and null space (Ax=0).

slides.title: Linear independence, basis, and dimension
bullets: Vectors are linearly independent when the only linear combination equal to the zero vector uses all zero coefficients.
A basis is a linearly independent set that spans the space.
Every basis of a given space has the same number of vectors, which is the space’s dimension.
slides.speakerNotes: Add the practical implications: basis gives unique coordinates, and dimension counts basis vector count, not the number of elements in the space.
slides.altText: A triangle of ideas: independence → basis → dimension, with arrows between them.

slides.title: Rank: how it links column space and null space
bullets: The rank of a matrix is the dimension of its column space, which equals the number of pivot columns.
The nullity is the dimension of its null space.
For an m-by-n matrix, rank plus nullity equals n, and row rank equals column rank.
slides.speakerNotes: Use this slide as a computational bridge: once you row-reduce, you read pivot columns (rank) and then infer nullity via rank-nullity.
slides.altText: A balance scale labeled “rank + nullity = n,” with pivot columns highlighted.

slides.title: Matrix algebra and multiplication: order matters
bullets: Matrix addition and scalar multiplication act entrywise, while the matrix product AB is defined when A’s columns match B’s rows.
The (i,j) entry of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B.
Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative, and it is associative and distributive over addition.
slides.speakerNotes: Warn students not to treat multiplication like addition. Also emphasize associativity and distributivity as tools for algebraic manipulation when factor order is preserved.
slides.altText: A diagram of row-by-column multiplication producing each entry of AB, with a note “AB ≠ BA in general.”

slides.title: Invertibility, inverses, and determinants
bullets: A square matrix A is invertible exactly when it has n pivots, equivalently when its determinant is nonzero.
If A is invertible, the system Ax = b has the unique solution x = A⁻¹b for every right-hand side b.
Determinant facts: det(AB) = det(A)det(B), and row operations affect the determinant predictably.
slides.speakerNotes: Keep this tightly linked: invertible ⇔ n pivots ⇔ det nonzero. Then remind that unique solvability for Ax=b is the computational payoff.
slides.altText: A flowchart: pivots ⇔ determinant nonzero ⇔ invertible ⇔ unique solution x = A^{-1}b.

slides.title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors in one sentence each
bullets: An eigenvector x of A satisfies Ax = λx with x nonzero, and λ is found as a root of det(A − λI).
Eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are automatically linearly independent.
An n-by-n matrix is diagonalizable exactly when it has n linearly independent eigenvectors.
slides.speakerNotes: Do not let students treat the zero vector as an eigenvector. Emphasize the definition: nonzero requirement and the characteristic polynomial.
slides.altText: A matrix A acting on a vector x scales it by λ, with a box for “characteristic polynomial det(A − λI).”

slides.title: Orthogonality, projections, and least squares: what problems want
bullets: Orthogonal vectors have dot product zero, and orthogonal/orthonormal bases simplify coordinates and projections.
A projection P satisfies P^2 = P, and it is an orthogonal projection iff it is symmetric and satisfies P^2 = P.
Least squares finds x̂ minimizing the residual b − Ax and corresponds to projecting b onto the column space of A.
slides.speakerNotes: Tie to computation goals: projection maps into the subspace, and least squares is the “closest residual” story with normal equations and column-space projection.
slides.altText: Three icons labeled orthogonality (dot product zero), projection (P^2=P), and least squares (best residual projection onto column space).

slides.title: Final exam readiness checklist
bullets: A final exam assesses mastery by requiring independent solution of problems under time constraints.
Scoring depends on both correctness and the clarity of intermediate steps required by the rubric.
Your work must justify derived conclusions and verify correctness for theorem-based computations by substitution.
slides.speakerNotes: Encourage students to structure solutions: write what you are doing, show key steps, and finish with checks when appropriate. Point them to the specific review habit: substitute back into defining equations.
slides.altText: A checklist titled “final exam readiness” with items: independent solution, correctness + clear steps, and justify plus substitute checks.

body.text: Start with the definition: a system of linear equations is a collection of linear equations in the same variables, and a solution assigns values to all variables so every equation holds at the same time. Classify systems by the number of solutions: exactly zero, exactly one, or infinitely many—never exactly two. Translate a couple of quick examples into “what it means geometrically” (meeting lines vs parallel lines) to make consistency/inconsistency feel concrete.

Move to augmented matrices as the compact representation. Explain that every linear system can be represented as an augmented matrix and solved by row reduction. Introduce echelon form vocabulary: pivot, pivot positions, and free vs basic variables (at the level of reading off solutions). Emphasize the reading: pivot positions determine which variables are constrained and which are free.

Worked example (from this week’s core idea): Solve a 2-equation system by row reduction and explicitly interpret the RREF. Example to walk through: x + y = 2 and x + y = 5. Convert to an augmented matrix, perform elementary row operations to reach echelon/RREF, then read off the outcome: the row 0 = 3 appears, so the system is inconsistent (no solutions). Along the way, make two checks: (1) row operations preserve the solution set, and (2) inconsistencies show up as a contradictory equation.

Mini-lab: In pairs, students get short systems and are asked two things without fully solving: (a) decide consistent vs inconsistent from the structure of equations (e.g., same left-hand side but different constants), and (b) if consistent, predict whether solutions are unique or infinitely many. Then students justify using the “zero/one/infinitely many” rule. Collect 2–3 representative student justifications and correct common reasoning.

Reteach pivot/row-operation reasoning with a targeted walkthrough of what students often mix up: show that elementary row operations do not change the solution set (swap, scale by nonzero, add multiple). Then show how pivot positions come from the echelon structure, not from “largest entry” thinking. Finish with a quick re-read: once you have echelon/RREF, pivot positions tell you which variables are basic and which are free.

body.prompt: Why is it valid to use elementary row operations to solve a system? Explain what must be preserved and why.
body.tension: Students often think the matrix “changes the equations” so the answers should change, but row operations are reversible and preserve the solution set.
followUps: What does it mean for a system to be consistent, and how could row reduction reveal that?
How do pivot positions relate to which variables become determined versus free?

body.task: Convert two given systems of linear equations into augmented matrices. For each system, perform row reduction to reach echelon form and then use pivot positions to determine solutions or conclude the system is inconsistent. Write your final answer clearly as “no solution,” “one solution,” or “infinitely many solutions,” and state the corresponding variable values when applicable.
steps: For each system, write its augmented matrix in the order the variables are given.
Use elementary row operations to reach echelon form and identify pivot positions.
Determine the solution status by reading the reduced information you get from the echelon form.
Check that your answer matches the required solution set type: 0, 1, or infinitely many.

rubricBands.observableBehavior: Student correctly states what a solution is and correctly classifies the system as consistent or inconsistent, including correct 0/1/infinitely many outcome.
Student correctly performs elementary row operations and identifies pivot positions, then uses pivot structure to determine which variables are basic versus free.
Student claims that row operations change the solutions or that pivot columns are determined by the largest numbers rather than by pivot positions from echelon structure.

body.q: Are pivot columns the ones with the largest entries?
body.a: No. Pivot positions are determined by echelon structure during elimination, not by the size of the entries.

body.text: Start with the idea of “vectors” as objects with two operations: addition and scalar multiplication. State the vector-space axioms at a high level (closure, identity/zero, inverses, distributivity, associativity, commutativity) and emphasize that the *definition* is algebraic, not geometric. Quick check: what is the zero vector’s role? what does it mean for a subset to be closed under operations?

Vectors beyond arrows: compare the standard example R^n with other vector-space examples (polynomials, matrices, functions) using the “anything satisfying the vector-space axioms is a vector” mindset. Then shift to linear combinations: given vectors v1,…,vk, a linear combination is a vector of the form c1 v1 + … + ck vk. Do a couple of coefficient substitution drills (no new theorems) to build fluency in forming combinations and interpreting them as “all possible scaled-adds.”

Worked example (from this week’s focus): Take vectors v1 = (1,2) and v2 = (3,0). Form the linear combination 2v1 - 3v2. Compute step-by-step: first scale (2v1) and (3v2), then add with the correct signs. Conclude with the final vector and interpret it as “the result of choosing coefficients.” Then connect back to vector-space closure: because scaling and adding vectors stays inside the space, the computed combination is a valid vector.

Mini-stations (quick pairs): (1) Decide whether a given subset can be a vector space (focus on zero vector + closure under addition and scalar multiplication). (2) Write down linear combinations that produce a target vector, when possible, by matching coefficients informally (no heavy solving yet). (3) Identify which “solution-count” statements are valid for linear systems: zero / one / infinitely many solutions; never exactly two. Students justify briefly with one sentence each.

Reteach a single confusion with a worked walk-through: use the corrective for inconsistent systems. Show the pair x + y = 1 and x + y = 3. Explain that subtracting the equations gives (x+y)-(x+y)=1-3 ⇒ 0=-2, which cannot happen for real numbers. Tie this to the rule: a linear system has exactly zero, one, or infinitely many solutions—never exactly two—and consistency means at least one solution exists.

body.prompt: Pick one vector-space statement and test it mentally against closure and the zero vector: would the set you have in mind still contain the zero vector after the operations? Then pick a linear system and decide whether it could be consistent or inconsistent using the idea of simultaneous satisfaction.
body.tension: Students often treat “it lives in R^n” as sufficient for being a vector space, and they also assume every linear system must have at least one solution.
followUps: Give a concrete example of a subset of R^n that fails to be a vector space and name exactly which requirement breaks.
Write a pair of linear equations that you believe is inconsistent, then explain why no assignment can satisfy both at once.

body.task: Form linear combinations of given vectors and check whether your results remain in the same vector-space setting. Then, for each linear system you are given, determine whether it must have zero, one, or infinitely many solutions (and label consistent vs inconsistent). Finally, explain your reasoning in terms of simultaneous satisfaction and the solution-count rules.
steps: Compute the requested linear combinations using scalar multiplication and addition, and write the resulting vectors explicitly.
State whether each described set is a vector space or fails to be one, referencing zero vector and closure under the operations.
For each linear system, decide consistency and the correct solution count category using only the given equations and the rules for zero/one/infinitely many solutions.
Write a short justification for each answer using complete sentences and the vocabulary “solution,” “consistent/inconsistent,” and “linear combination.”

rubricBands.observableBehavior: Student correctly computes a linear combination by carrying out scalar multiplication and addition, and matches the result to the stated vector-space setting.
Student correctly classifies each linear system as having zero, one, or infinitely many solutions and labels it consistent or inconsistent, using simultaneous satisfaction.
Student claims an arbitrary subset of R^n is automatically a vector space, or claims a linear system must always have a solution, or claims two solutions implies exactly two solutions.

body.q: Do vectors have to be arrows in 2D or 3D space?
body.a: No. A vector is any object that fits into a vector space with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the axioms, and examples include polynomials, matrices, and functions.

body.text: Warm-up: matrix algebra vs entrywise operations. We will distinguish (1) addition and scalar multiplication acting entrywise, from (2) the matrix product AB being defined only when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B. Then we connect definition to computation: the (i,j) entry of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. Quick mini-checks: “Is AB defined?” and “What does the (i,j) entry mean?”

Noncommutativity and order discipline. We focus on the idea that matrix multiplication is generally not commutative: AB and BA can differ, and one product may not even be defined. Students practice reading shapes and then predicting (at least qualitatively) whether AB=BA could hold, without doing full multiplication every time.

Worked example (from the reading’s theme): compute a specific entry using the dot-product rule for AB. We take two compatible matrices A and B and compute (2,3) of AB by: (i) identify row 2 of A, (ii) identify column 3 of B, (iii) take their dot product to get the (2,3) entry. Then we repeat for one more entry to reinforce the pattern (rows of A with columns of B). Emphasis: this is not entrywise multiplication; it’s dot products.

Guided practice with mixed prompts: (a) decide whether products are defined using dimensions, (b) compute one or two entries of AB using row–column dot products, (c) answer conceptual multiple-choice about commutativity and associativity/distributivity with order preserved (no swapping factors). Students justify each choice in 1 sentence.

Reteach: connect row reduction ideas to reliability (reversibility + pivots). Even though we are currently on matrix multiplication, today’s mistakes often spill into elimination. We walk through what students should remember: each elementary row operation is reversible and preserves the solution set—this is exactly why elimination is valid. Then we re-emphasize pivot positions come from echelon structure during elimination, not from the “largest numbers” in the matrix.

body.prompt: When you compute (AB)_{i,j}, what two objects do you use, and how are they combined?
body.tension: Students often expect multiplication to work “like addition,” but matrix multiplication is built from row–column dot products and depends on factor order and sizes.
followUps: Give the size condition for when AB is defined.
Name one reason AB and BA can fail to be equal.
Explain why elementary row operations are still allowed when solving linear systems.

body.task: Compute two valid matrix products using the dot-product definition: first compute AB, then compute BA only if it is defined. For each product, show how you compute at least two entries using dot products of rows of the left matrix with columns of the right matrix. Finally, write one sentence explaining whether commutativity held and why that happens.
steps: Choose matrices A and B with dimensions that make AB defined, then compute AB entry-by-entry using (i,j) entries as row–column dot products.
Compute BA as well if the dimension condition allows it, and compare the results.
For at least two entries in each computed product, show the dot-product calculation explicitly.
Conclude with a short explanation tied to dimension matching and non-commutativity.

rubricBands.observableBehavior: Student computes matrix products using the entry rule: each (i,j) entry is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B, and the student checks the dimension condition for when AB is defined.
Student correctly states and uses that matrix multiplication is generally not commutative, and preserves factor order when rewriting expressions like A(B + C).
Student multiplies matrices entrywise as if AB_{i,j} were computed directly from A_{i,j} and B_{i,j}, or assumes AB = BA without checking definitions or dimension compatibility.

body.q: Can I always swap the order and say AB = BA?
body.a: No. Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative, so AB and BA can differ, and one of the products may not be defined.

body.text: Start from the definition: an n-by-n matrix A is invertible if there exists a matrix B such that AB = BA = I. Emphasize uniqueness of the inverse (so we write A⁻¹) and the practical meaning: if A is invertible, then for every b the system Ax = b has the unique solution x = A⁻¹b.

Invertibility criteria and what can’t happen: only square matrices can be invertible; even square matrices fail when their columns are linearly dependent. Connect this to the “exactly when A has n pivots (equivalently, nonzero determinant)” viewpoint, but keep the logic grounded in existence of B with AB = BA = I.

Worked example (from today’s reading-style task): Decide whether A is invertible and, if so, compute x from a system. Use the workflow: (1) check A is square, (2) determine whether A has n pivots (equivalently nonzero determinant / columns not linearly dependent), (3) if invertible, use x = A⁻¹b. Then explicitly verify the defining property by checking AB = I and BA = I for the computed inverse. (Name the worked example: “Decide invertibility and solve Ax=b using x=A⁻¹b.”)

Matrix algebra quick-checks that feed invertibility: (a) identity on both sides matters, (b) order matters in products, (c) undoing composed operations reverses order. Students do short prompts: given a product AB, write the correct formula for (AB)⁻¹ when both inverses exist; and compare AB vs BA with a reason why they might differ.

Re-teach the inverse-of-a-product and the “nonzero but not invertible” misconception trap. Walk through two mini-cases: (1) why a square matrix with two equal rows has zero determinant so it is nonzero yet has no inverse; (2) why (AB)⁻¹ is not A⁻¹B⁻¹ but instead requires reversing order: (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹. Tie both back to the definition AB = BA = I.

body.prompt: A student claims: “Every nonzero matrix has an inverse.” What is the smallest correction you can make using only the definition of invertible and the pivot condition?
body.tension: The student is using 'nonzero' as if it were the same as 'invertible,' but invertibility is about having n pivots (equivalently nonzero determinant) and about the existence of AB=BA=I.
followUps: Can you point to a specific square matrix shape or property that prevents AB=BA=I from happening?
How does 'two equal rows' relate to having n pivots and to having a nonzero determinant?
If a matrix were invertible, what would be guaranteed about Ax=b for every right-hand side b?

body.task: For each given 2-by-2 or 3-by-3 matrix A, determine whether it is invertible using the pivot condition (n pivots). If A is invertible, compute A⁻¹ and then verify by checking that AB = BA = I for B = A⁻¹. Finally, pick one vector b and solve Ax=b using x=A⁻¹b, then confirm the solution by multiplying back.
steps: Decide invertibility by checking whether A has n pivots and state the correct conclusion.
If invertible, find A⁻¹ and write the explicit inverse matrix.
Verify the inverse by computing both AB and BA and checking they equal I.
Use x=A⁻¹b for a chosen b and verify that Ax=b holds.

rubricBands.observableBehavior: The student checks invertibility via n pivots (or equivalently nonzero determinant) and correctly uses the definition AB=BA=I to justify the inverse.
The student computes A⁻¹ when it exists, verifies both AB=I and BA=I, and solves Ax=b by x=A⁻¹b with a correct multiplication check.
The student claims every nonzero matrix has an inverse or uses (AB)⁻¹=A⁻¹B⁻¹ instead of reversing order to (AB)⁻¹=B⁻¹A⁻¹.

body.q: Why do we require AB = BA = I, not just AB = I?
body.a: Invertibility is defined by both AB = I and BA = I for the same B. That makes B the (unique) inverse A⁻¹ and ensures the inverse works on both sides.

body.q: What is the correct rule for inverting a product?
body.a: If both inverses exist, the correct rule is (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹. The order must reverse because you are undoing the composition.

body.text: Determinants as a single-number test of invertibility and a volume/area scaling factor. Start with: for a square matrix, “nonzero exactly when the matrix is invertible” and abs(det) scales area/volume under the transformation. Connect this to the practical criterion: A is invertible iff det(A) is nonzero.

Determinant properties we’ll use in computation. (1) Multiplicativity: det(AB)=det(A)det(B). (2) Row operations: swapping rows flips sign; scaling a row scales the determinant; adding a multiple of one row to another leaves it unchanged. Emphasize what is predictable vs what is not (especially additivity).

Worked example re-teach (row operations): Use row-reduction style reasoning to compute a determinant by transforming to an easy matrix. Walk through this exact workflow: (a) Start with a 3 3 matrix A. (b) Apply a row swap to create zeros—track the sign flip. (c) Scale a row to make a pivot—track the scaling factor. (d) Use row replacement (add a multiple of one row to another) to clear entries—track that the determinant is unchanged by these additions. (e) Conclude with det(A) from the final upper-triangular (product of diagonal) you reached using only the allowed row-operation effects. Students who came in cold: pay attention to the determinant bookkeeping at each step.

Concept check rotation: short paired problems where students decide which determinant rule applies (additivity vs multiplicativity; row operation effects; invertibility via nonzero determinant). Students must justify in one sentence using a rule statement.

Tie-in to common misconceptions and quick bridge to inverses/subspaces: (1) why det(A+B) isn’t det(A)+det(B); (2) why small entries don’t imply small determinants; (3) geometry is a model, not the definition of vectors; (4) subsets aren’t automatically vector spaces unless they contain 0 and are closed under + and scalar multiplication.

body.prompt: Think about two different ways the determinant can be “controlled”: (1) through row operations with predictable sign/scale/invariance effects, and (2) through the equivalence between det(A) ≠ 0 and invertibility. Can you explain which determinant facts you would use first to decide whether a matrix is invertible without fully computing the determinant?
body.tension: Students often try to estimate determinant size from entry size, but the determinant’s reliable meaning here is about invertibility and how row operations change it in exact ways.
followUps: Which row operations would you choose to simplify a matrix while tracking how det changes?
How does the product rule det(AB)=det(A)det(B) help when a matrix can be written as a product?
What concrete reason shows that det(A+B) is generally not equal to det(A)+det(B)?

body.task: Compute the determinant of two 2×2 or 3×3 matrices using row operations, and justify each step by stating how the determinant changes under the operation used. For at least one matrix, determine whether it is invertible using the nonzero/nonzero determinant criterion. In addition, rewrite one incorrect claim you have seen (such as det(A + B) = det(A) + det(B) or “small entries imply small determinant”) into a correct statement using the rules from class.
steps: Perform a sequence of row operations to transform each matrix into an easy-to-read form, and track the determinant sign and scaling from each operation.
Compute the determinant from the resulting matrix (using the determinant’s behavior under your tracked operations).
State whether each matrix is invertible by checking whether the determinant is nonzero.
Correct one misconception by replacing it with the correct determinant rule or interpretation.

rubricBands.observableBehavior: Student correctly states that a square matrix is invertible if and only if its determinant is nonzero, and applies this to at least one computed determinant.

Student uses at least two correct row-operation rules (swap sign flip, scaling scales determinant, adding a multiple leaves it unchanged) and arrives at the correct determinant value for both matrices.
Student claims det(A + B) = det(A) + det(B) or concludes that determinant magnitude tracks entry size, and this directly leads to incorrect determinant or invertibility conclusions.

body.q: If swapping rows flips the sign of the determinant, what happens if I swap the same pair twice?
body.a: Swapping two rows flips the sign, so doing the same swap twice flips the sign twice and returns the determinant to its original sign.

body.q: Does det(A) tell us anything besides whether A is invertible?
body.a: Yes: the absolute value of det(A) scales area or volume under the matrix’s transformation, not the size of the entries.

body.text: Warm-up on what a vector space really is: a set + operations that satisfy the axioms (closure, associativity, commutativity, identity, inverses, distributivity). Emphasize: geometry is not the definition—polynomials, matrices, and functions can be vectors (under the usual operations).

Subspaces as a filter: given a vector space V, a subset W is a subspace only if it contains the zero vector and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication. Quick boundary checks: ‘Does scaling keep you inside?’ ‘Is the zero forced?’

Worked example (from the reading): Use the fact that the span of a set of vectors is the smallest subspace containing them. Take a set like {v1, v2}; write what span(v1, v2) means (all linear combinations αv1 + βv2), then show it is a subspace by checking: it contains 0 (use α=β=0) and it is closed under addition/scaling (combine coefficients).

Mini-labs (pairs): Decide whether each candidate subset is a subspace, justify with the three subspace requirements (zero + closure under addition + closure under scalar multiplication). One problem targets the misconception ‘a line/plane in R^3 is always a subspace’; another targets ‘span of two vectors is always a plane.’

Reteach for students who arrived cold: walk the same worked example again with extra emphasis on definitions. We start from span(v1, v2) = {αv1 + βv2}. Then we explicitly prove it is a subspace: (1) zero vector is included by choosing α=β=0, (2) if u=αv1+βv2 and w=γv1+δv2 then u+w=(α+γ)v1+(β+δ)v2 is still in the span, (3) for scalar k, ku=(kα)v1+(kβ)v2 stays in the span. Finish by connecting this to why a ‘line not through the origin’ fails: scaling takes you out and/or it misses the zero vector.

body.prompt: Take two sets and decide whether each is a vector space or a subspace. First, consider the subset of R^2 consisting only of vectors on the line x = 1. Second, consider a span: if you choose two vectors in R^3, what must always be true about the set of all their linear combinations?
body.tension: Students often rely on geometry (“it looks like a line/plane”), but the definition depends on containing zero and being closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
followUps: Which specific requirement fails for the set x = 1, and does it fail because of missing zero or because of scaling leaving the set?
For the span of two vectors in R^3, what can make the span shrink to a line or point?
How does the “smallest subspace containing the generators” viewpoint help you avoid guessing?

body.task: For each case below, decide whether the set is a vector space, a subspace, or neither, and justify using the zero vector and closure under addition and scalar multiplication. Then compute a span in one of the cases by writing the general linear combination and describing the resulting set. Your justification should explicitly refer to what happens when you add and scale vectors in the set. Conclude by stating what span tells you about the “smallest subspace” interpretation.
steps: Case A: Determine whether the subset of R^2 defined by x = 1 is a subspace of R^2 and explain why using zero and closure.
Case B: Determine whether the set of all polynomials of degree at most 2 is a vector space under the usual addition and scalar multiplication.
Case C: Choose S = { (1, 2, 0), (0, 0, 1) } in R^3 and compute span(S) by writing a general linear combination and simplifying.
Briefly state whether your computed span is the smallest subspace containing the given generators and explain why in one sentence.

rubricBands.observableBehavior: The student applies the definition of a subspace by checking that zero is included and that the set is closed under addition and scalar multiplication, and they completes at least one span computation with an explicit linear-combination form.

The student gives a mostly correct decision with partial justification, such as mentioning closure but not clearly addressing zero, or computing a span but describing it without fully simplifying the linear combinations.
The student claims that any line or plane in R^3 is automatically a subspace, or claims that any subset of R^n is automatically a vector space, without checking zero or closure.

slides.title: Week 6 goal: recognize vector spaces and subspaces
bullets: A vector space is a set where addition and scalar multiplication are always valid inside the set.
A subspace is a subset that is itself a vector space under the same operations.
R^n is the standard example, but it is not the only one.
slides.speakerNotes: We will use the axioms/closure idea as a checklist: vector space first, then subspace. Keep in mind that vectors need not be arrows.
slides.altText: Checklist-style introduction to vector spaces and subspaces.

slides.title: What makes a vector space?
bullets: A vector space is a set of vectors with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the axioms.
Closure and distributivity are part of the axioms, not optional extras.
Every vector space must contain a zero vector and each vector must have an additive inverse.
slides.speakerNotes: Focus students on the “must contain zero” and “must stay closed under operations” parts, because those are the most commonly missed.
slides.altText: Bulleted list of the key vector space requirements including zero and additive inverses.

slides.title: Examples: not just geometric arrows
bullets: A vector space must satisfy the vector-space axioms, not a picture in 2D or 3D.
Polynomials form a vector space under the usual addition and scalar multiplication.
Matrices form a vector space under entrywise addition and scalar multiplication.
slides.speakerNotes: Use this to directly counter the “vectors are always arrows” mindset. Geometry is a model, but the definition is algebraic.
slides.altText: Examples of vector spaces beyond arrow geometry: polynomials and matrices.

slides.title: Closure matters for subsets
bullets: A subset of a vector space can fail to be a vector space if it is not closed under operations.
If you add two members of a subset or scale one member and leave the subset, it is not a vector space.
slides.speakerNotes: This sets up the subspace test: zero plus closure under addition and scaling.
slides.altText: Illustration of a subset that is not closed under addition or scaling.

slides.title: Subspaces: the test you can apply
bullets: A subspace is a subset of a vector space that contains the zero vector.
A subspace is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
If a subset passes these checks, it is a vector space and we call it a subspace.
slides.speakerNotes: State the subspace checklist plainly; students will reuse it repeatedly later.
slides.altText: Subspace definition framed as a checklist: zero, closure under addition, closure under scaling.

slides.title: Span always gives a subspace
bullets: The span of a set of vectors means all their linear combinations.
The span is always a subspace because it contains zero and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
The span of a set is the smallest subspace containing those vectors.
slides.speakerNotes: Connect “span” to “linear combinations” so students see why span automatically works as a subspace.
slides.altText: Span as all linear combinations, yielding the smallest containing subspace.

slides.title: Worked example: compute a span
bullets: A general linear combination is a(1, 0) + b(0, 1) = (a, b).
All pairs (a, b) occur, so span(S) = R^2, which is a subspace.
slides.speakerNotes: Show the explicit computation of the set of linear combinations and conclude it is closed and contains zero by construction.
slides.altText: Concrete computation showing span of (1,0) and (0,1) equals all of R^2.

slides.title: Misconception check: subspaces must pass the zero test
bullets: Only lines and planes through the origin can be subspaces in R^3.
If a line or plane does not contain the zero vector, it cannot be a subspace.
If scaling a vector leaves the set, closure fails and it is not a subspace.
slides.speakerNotes: Directly address the “any line or plane in R^3 is a subspace” misconception using the zero and closure requirements.
slides.altText: Warn that lines/planes not through the origin miss the zero vector and fail closure.

slides.title: Misconception check: span of two vectors is not always a plane
bullets: The span of two vectors is the set of all their linear combinations.
If the two vectors are parallel (or one is zero), their span collapses to a line or point.
So the result depends on whether the vectors are independent.
slides.speakerNotes: Emphasize that span is generated by linear combinations; dimension is not guaranteed just because there are two generators.
slides.altText: Illustration that parallel generators produce a lower-dimensional span than a plane.

slides.title: Reminder: vector spaces can be described by operations, not pictures
bullets: A vector space can be any collection closed under addition and scalar multiplication with zero and inverses.
A subspace is the same idea applied to a subset of vectors.
When in doubt, test zero plus closure under addition and scaling.
slides.speakerNotes: Close with a simple decision rule students can apply quickly on homework and quizzes.
slides.altText: Summary decision rule for identifying vector spaces and subspaces.

body.text: Start with the definition: what it means for a set of vectors to be linearly independent (only the trivial combination gives the zero vector). Emphasize the contrast: a nontrivial combination equal to zero is a dependence relation. Quick mental check: what happens if the set contains the zero vector? (It’s automatically dependent.)

Move to the two practical tests students use in problems: (1) independence vs dependence “redundancy” idea (“dependent exactly when some vector is a linear combination of the others”), and (2) matrix viewpoint: columns of A are independent exactly when Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution (pivot columns). Tie both to the same theme: no redundancy.

Worked example (from the reading): Use the span/subspace connection to motivate basis and dimension. Go through this worked idea: determine whether a set of vectors forms a basis by checking two things—(i) linear independence and (ii) spanning. Then show how dimension is the fixed number of vectors in any basis (not the number of vectors you happened to start with). Concretely, illustrate with an R^n situation where you start with more vectors than needed and explain that dependence is forced by having too many vectors for the space.

Mini-station practice (group of 2): Students get 3 short prompts; each asks them to decide independence/dependence or basis/dimension. They must justify in words using the correct definition phrasing (e.g., “only the trivial coefficients make the zero vector” or “a vector is a linear combination of the others”). Instructor circulates and targets the common misconceptions: independent vs different, ‘more vectors = more independent,’ and ‘dimension = number of vectors.’

Reteach worked example: “Parallel vectors collapse the span.” Take two vectors that are parallel (or one is zero) and explicitly list a dependence relation showing the span is not a plane. Then connect directly to the claim: the span’s dimension depends on independence—if the vectors are dependent, you only get a lower-dimensional span.

body.prompt: Take a set of vectors and decide whether it is independent by using the “only trivial combination gives zero” rule or the “one vector is a combination of the others” rule. Then ask what you would need to upgrade it to a basis: independence plus spanning. Finally, connect your answer to dimension by stating how many vectors are in any basis of the same space.
body.tension: Students often think independence is about vectors being “different,” but dependence can happen even when every vector looks distinct.
followUps: Find an example where vectors are pairwise different but the set is dependent, and explain which redundancy relation creates the dependence.
Given two independent vectors in R^2, explain what happens if you add a third vector that can be written as a linear combination of the first two.
For an n-vector set in R^n, explain how spanning and independence force each other.

body.task: For each part below, determine whether the given set of vectors is linearly independent or dependent, and justify your answer using the definition or the “vector is a combination of the others” rule. Then decide whether the set is a basis for the relevant vector space, and state the dimension implied by your basis count. If you conclude the set is not a basis, specify what property fails (independence or spanning) in your own words.
steps: Part 1: Determine independence of the given vectors by finding or ruling out a nontrivial linear combination that equals the zero vector.
Part 2: If the set is dependent, identify a concrete dependence relation expressing one vector as a linear combination of the others.
Part 3: For the space you are given, determine whether your independent set spans; conclude whether it is a basis.
Part 4: State the dimension using the basis size rule, and explain why other bases must have the same number of vectors.

rubricBands.observableBehavior: The student correctly uses the independence criterion (only the all-zero coefficients produce the zero vector) or correctly identifies a dependence relation by expressing one vector as a linear combination of the others, and then clearly connects this to basis (independent and spanning).

The student reaches the correct independence/dependence and basis/dimension conclusions but justification is incomplete, such as stating a relation without confirming nontriviality, or mentioning spanning/independence without stating how it follows.

The student argues independence because vectors are “different from each other,” or argues more vectors automatically means “more independence,” or confuses dimension with the total number of vectors rather than the size of any basis.

body.q: Does a vector space have only one basis, and is its dimension just the number of its vectors?
body.a: A vector space has infinitely many bases in general; what is fixed is the number of vectors in any basis. Dimension is that basis size, not the total number of vectors in the space.

slides.title: Where we are in Week 7
bullets: We will connect linear independence, basis, and dimension.
These ideas all live inside a vector space or a subspace of it.
slides.speakerNotes: Today’s goal is to use the definitions to decide independence, identify bases, and compute dimension by counting basis vectors.
slides.altText: A roadmap showing three connected boxes: Linear independence → Basis → Dimension.

slides.title: Linear independence: the definition
bullets: A set of vectors is linearly independent when the only linear combination equal to the zero vector uses all zero coefficients.
A nontrivial linear combination equal to the zero vector is a linear dependence relation.
slides.speakerNotes: Keep the logical structure: independence means there are no nontrivial solutions to a zero-combination equation.
slides.altText: A definition box describing zero linear combinations and the word “nontrivial”.

slides.title: Quick dependence checks
bullets: A set containing the zero vector is automatically linearly dependent.
A set of vectors is dependent exactly when some vector in it is a linear combination of the others.
slides.speakerNotes: This gives fast ways to rule out independence: either the zero vector is present, or you can write one vector using the rest.
slides.altText: Two checkmarks labeled “contains zero vector” and “one vector is a combination of the others.”

slides.title: Independence and matrices
bullets: The columns of a matrix A are independent exactly when Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution.
Having only the trivial solution means every column is a pivot column.
slides.speakerNotes: We will use this perspective when independence is asked for columns of a matrix: solve Ax = 0 and check whether any free variable appears.
slides.altText: A matrix A with its columns highlighted, alongside an arrow to “Ax = 0 only trivial solution.”

slides.title: Worked example: independence vs dependence
bullets: The three vectors are dependent because v3 = v1 + v2.
slides.speakerNotes: This example also addresses a common confusion: the vectors are pairwise different, but dependence comes from redundancy (one vector can be formed from the others).
slides.altText: Three points (vectors) in R^2 showing v3 equals the sum of v1 and v2.

slides.title: Worked example conclusion
bullets: The set {v1, v2} is linearly independent because the only way a v1 + b v2 equals the zero vector is a = b = 0.
The full set {v1, v2, v3} is dependent since there exists a nontrivial zero relation: v1 + v2 − v3 = 0.
slides.speakerNotes: We have a clean contrast: two vectors in R^2 can be independent, but adding a redundant third vector forces dependence.
slides.altText: An equation sheet showing a v1 + b v2 = 0 implies a=b=0, and v1+v2−v3=0 as a nontrivial relation.

slides.title: Basis: independence plus spanning
bullets: A basis of a vector space is a linearly independent set that spans the space.
Any basis of a given space has the same number of vectors, and that common count is the space’s dimension.
slides.speakerNotes: To be a basis you need both parts: independence prevents redundancy, and spanning guarantees you can build every vector.
slides.altText: A two-part Venn diagram labeled “linearly independent” and “spans the space.”

slides.title: Coordinates in a basis
bullets: Every vector in the space is a unique linear combination of basis vectors.
The coefficients in that unique combination are the vector’s coordinates in that basis.
slides.speakerNotes: When basis vectors are used as “building blocks,” uniqueness tells you there is exactly one coefficient set for each vector.
slides.altText: A basis vectors bundle labeled and a vector decomposed uniquely into coefficients.

slides.title: Dimension in practice (what to count)
bullets: All bases of a finite-dimensional vector space contain the same number of vectors.
In R^n, any n independent vectors form a basis.
slides.speakerNotes: We often compute dimension by identifying a basis and then counting its vectors, or by using the R^n independence/basis shortcut.
slides.altText: A counting view of basis size in R^n, with n independent vectors highlighted.

slides.title: Spanning sets and independence in R^n
bullets: In R^n, any spanning set of n vectors is automatically independent.
So in R^n, an n-vector set is a basis exactly when it is either independent or spanning.
slides.speakerNotes: This is a common workflow: prove independence to get spanning, or prove spanning to get independence, and then conclude basis and dimension via the fixed size n.
slides.altText: Two arrows between “independent” and “spanning” for n vectors in R^n, meeting at “basis.”

body.markdown:
## Week 8 Midterm Quick Study Guide (Systems → Subspaces)

### Core definitions (you should be able to state/recognize these)
- **Subspace**: A subset of a vector space that **contains the zero vector** and is **closed under addition** and **scalar multiplication**.
- **Span**: For vectors v1, …, vk, **span{v1,…,vk}** is the set of **all linear combinations**. The span is **the smallest subspace containing those vectors**.
- **Consistent vs inconsistent system**: **Consistent** means **at least one solution exists**; **inconsistent** means **no solution exists**.
- **Row reduction + elementary operations**: Elementary row operations (swap, scale by nonzero, add a multiple of one row to another) **preserve the solution set**, which is why elimination works.

### Misconceptions to watch for (read these as “do not do this”)
1) **Subspace shape trap**: “Any line or plane in R^3 is a subspace.”
   - Correct idea: **Only lines and planes through the origin are subspaces**; others miss the zero vector and are not closed under scaling.
2) **Span-of-two trap**: “The span of two vectors is always a plane.”
   - Correct idea: If the two vectors are **parallel (or one is zero)**, their span collapses to a **line or a point**; the span’s dimension depends on independence.
3) **Systems trap (solutions)**: “Every system of equations has a solution.”
   - Correct idea: A system like **x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent** (parallel lines that never meet).
4) **Solutions count trap**: “If a system has more than one solution, it has some finite number of them.”
   - Correct idea: Over the reals, **once a linear system has two distinct solutions it has infinitely many** (the whole line through the two solutions solves the system).

### Self-check prompts
- If I give you a set like L = {(x,y,z) : x = 1, y = 0} (a line not through the origin), can you quickly verify the **zero vector test** and **scaling closure**?
- When you see a row-reduced augmented matrix, can you tell whether it contains a contradiction row (which means **inconsistent**)?
- For two vectors v and w, can you decide whether span{v,w} is a **line, point, or plane** based on whether v and w are independent?

### If you missed the reading
If you missed the reading, focus on the two decision rules: (1) a **subspace must contain 0 and be closed under addition/scalar multiplication**, and (2) a linear system has **0, 1, or infinitely many** solutions (never exactly two). Then connect row reduction to consistency: the only thing that matters for classification is what the reduced augmented matrix implies about contradictions. Finally, remember that **span** is all linear combinations and the **dimension depends on independence** (parallel/zero vectors reduce the span).

body.q: How do I tell whether something is a subspace quickly?
body.a: Use the subspace checklist: it must contain the zero vector, be closed under addition, and be closed under scalar multiplication.
