assets.conceptName: midterm exam covering systems through subspaces

slides.title: Midterm scope: from systems to subspaces
bullets: This midterm covers systems of linear equations through subspaces.
A linear system can be represented by an augmented matrix and solved by row reduction.
The column space of a matrix A is the span of its columns.
The null space of a matrix A is the set of solutions to Ax = 0.
slides.speakerNotes: Set expectations for what students must connect: solutions of systems are tied to consistency, row reduction, and spans (column space) and homogeneous solutions (null space).
slides.altText: Agenda slide listing four core midterm topics: consistency and augmented matrices, row reduction, column space as a span, and null space as Ax = 0 solutions.

slides.title: Systems: solutions come in three types
bullets: A system of linear equations is a collection of linear equations in the same variables.
A solution assigns values to every variable so all equations hold simultaneously.
A linear system has exactly zero, one, or infinitely many solutions.
A system is consistent when at least one solution exists and inconsistent when no solution exists.
slides.speakerNotes: Emphasize the “three possibilities” rule: students should reject “exactly two” as impossible for linear systems over the reals.
slides.altText: Slide showing the definitions of solution, consistency, and the rule that linear systems have 0, 1, or infinitely many solutions.

slides.title: Augmented matrices and solving by row reduction
bullets: Every linear system can be represented compactly as an augmented matrix.
Row reduction uses elementary row operations: swap, scale, and add multiples of rows.
Elementary row operations do not change the solution set of the represented system.
The reduced row echelon form is unique, even though different elimination paths can be used.
slides.speakerNotes: Tie row reduction to “reading off” solutions later, and connect uniqueness to students’ need for a consistent final form.
slides.altText: Slide describing augmented matrices, elementary row operations, invariance of the solution set, and uniqueness of reduced row echelon form.

slides.title: Pivot idea: basic vs free variables
bullets: In echelon form, a pivot is the first nonzero entry of a row.
Pivot positions determine which variables are basic and which are free.
Different sequences of row operations can reach the same reduced row echelon form.
Pivot positions are determined by the elimination structure, not by entry sizes.
slides.speakerNotes: Students often try to pick pivots by “largest numbers”; steer them to the structural definition and the echelon pattern.
slides.altText: Slide defining pivots in echelon form and explaining that pivot positions determine basic and free variables.

slides.title: Worked example: inconsistency and “not exactly two solutions”
bullets: Consider the system x + y = 1 and x + y = 3.
These two equations cannot both be true for any real x and y.
So the system has zero solutions and is inconsistent.
Over the reals, a linear system never has exactly two solutions.
slides.speakerNotes: Concrete mismatch of right-hand sides illustrates inconsistency directly. Also reinforces the “0, 1, or infinitely many” rule in an example-focused way.
slides.altText: Slide with the explicit system x+y=1 and x+y=3 and the conclusion that it has zero solutions, hence is inconsistent.

slides.title: Vector spaces: what vectors must satisfy
bullets: A vector space is a set with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the vector-space axioms.
A vector space must contain the zero vector and include additive inverses for every vector.
R^n is the standard example of a vector space.
Vector spaces need not be geometric arrows: polynomials, matrices, and functions can form vector spaces.
slides.speakerNotes: Prepare students to recognize vectors as algebraic objects. This matters when questions about spans and closures use non-geometric “vectors.”
slides.altText: Slide listing the vector space axioms at a high level and noting that vector spaces can be polynomials, matrices, or functions.

slides.title: Subspaces: the closure tests
bullets: A subspace is a subset of a vector space that contains the zero vector.
A subspace is closed under addition.
A subspace is closed under scalar multiplication.
The span of a set of vectors is always a subspace.
slides.speakerNotes: Make the checklist explicit: zero vector plus closure under addition and scaling. Then connect to span as the “automatic subspace” construction.
slides.altText: Slide defining subspaces with three conditions and stating that spans are always subspaces.

slides.title: Span: smallest subspace containing the vectors
bullets: The span of a set of vectors is the set of all their linear combinations.
The span of a set of vectors is the smallest subspace containing them.
Linear combinations are formed using scalar weights applied to the vectors.
Because the span is a subspace, it is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
slides.speakerNotes: Even if students forget the formal definition, they should remember: span = all linear combinations and it is the minimal subspace containing those vectors.
slides.altText: Slide stating span as all linear combinations and as the smallest subspace containing a given set of vectors.

slides.title: Misconception check: lines and planes in R^3
bullets: Only lines and planes through the origin are subspaces.
A line or plane not through the origin misses the zero vector.
A subset that misses the zero vector cannot be a subspace.
Closure under scalar multiplication fails for sets not containing the origin.
slides.speakerNotes: Directly address the common misconception using the zero-vector criterion; this is one of the highest-yield conceptual errors for subspaces.
slides.altText: Slide warning that subspaces must contain the zero vector, so only lines/planes through the origin qualify.

slides.title: Misconception check: span of two vectors
bullets: The span of two vectors need not be a plane.
If the two vectors are parallel or one is zero, their span collapses to a line or a point.
The span’s dimension depends on whether the vectors are independent.
So you cannot assume the span always has the same dimension.
slides.speakerNotes: Reinforce that “two vectors” does not automatically mean “2D plane.” Students must reason using dependence/independence and linear combinations.
slides.altText: Slide explaining that the span of two vectors depends on independence and can be a line or point instead of a plane.

slides.title: Column space and consistency
bullets: The column space of a matrix A is the span of its columns.
The column space consists exactly of those b for which Ax = b is consistent.
So b is in the column space exactly when the system Ax = b has at least one solution.
If b is not in the column space, then Ax = b is inconsistent.
slides.speakerNotes: This is the bridge between “systems” and “subspaces”: membership in column space is a consistency test.
slides.altText: Slide linking column space membership of b with consistency of Ax=b.

slides.title: Null space: solutions to the homogeneous system
bullets: The null space of a matrix A is the set of solutions to Ax = 0.
The null space is a subspace of the domain.
So it contains the zero vector solution and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
Thinking in terms of subspaces helps organize all homogeneous solutions.
slides.speakerNotes: Connect directly to the subspace definition: homogeneous solutions automatically form a subspace.
slides.altText: Slide defining the null space as Ax=0 solutions and noting it is a subspace.

slides.title: Matrix operations and inversion (final facts to remember)
bullets: Matrix multiplication AB is defined when A has as many columns as B has rows.
The (i,j) entry of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B.
Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative, so AB and BA can differ.
An n-by-n matrix A is invertible exactly when it has n pivots, equivalently a nonzero determinant.
slides.speakerNotes: End with a compact reminder of multiplication definition and invertibility criteria, since midterms often test these alongside solution uniqueness.
slides.altText: Slide summarizing the definition of matrix multiplication, non-commutativity, and the invertibility criterion via pivots/nonzero determinant.

body.text: Warm-up on subspaces and spans: state the subspace test (must contain 0; closed under addition + scalar multiplication) and remind students that the span of vectors is the smallest subspace containing them. Quick check: why a “line not through the origin” fails the subspace test (doesn’t contain the zero vector and isn’t closed under scaling).

Column space: define it as the span of the columns of A, and interpret it via Ax=b. Emphasize: the column space consists exactly of those b for which Ax=b is consistent. Then connect null space: solutions to Ax=0, which is automatically a subspace of the domain.

Worked example (from today’s reading): use a matrix A and form the augmented system Ax=b. Do row reduction to decide whether b is consistent; then match the consistent b-values with the column space (span of columns). Finally, set b=0 to describe the null space as the solution set of Ax=0, and interpret rank as the dimension of the column space.

Concept-mapping activity: groups label three objects for the same matrix A: (1) column space = span(columns) = {b : Ax=b is consistent}, (2) null space = {x : Ax=0}, (3) rank = dim(column space) = number of pivots after row reduction. Students also do quick subspace checks on candidate “lines/planes” to reinforce origin-through requirement.

Reteach path (worked example walk-through for students who arrived cold): take the reading’s same setup idea—pick a generic Ax=b system and row-reduce. Step 1: row-reduce A|b and read consistency (either there is a contradiction like 0=nonzero, or there isn’t). Step 2: if consistent, connect that b to the column space definition: b must be in the span of columns. Step 3: set b=0 to get Ax=0 and identify the null space as a subspace. Step 4: rank is the number of pivot columns you see after row reduction (not “how many nonzero entries” you start with).

body.prompt: Pick a matrix A and describe what b must look like for Ax = b to have at least one solution. Then describe what x must look like for Ax = 0 to hold.
body.tension: Students often mix up “any line through the origin” with “any line or plane,” and they often think rank is about counting visible nonzero entries rather than dimension/pivots.
followUps: How does the set of solvable right-hand sides b relate to the span of A’s columns?
Why must the null space contain the zero vector and be closed under scaling and addition?
If you know the rank, how could you deduce the nullity when you also know the number of columns n?

body.task: For the matrix A = [[1, 2, 0], [0, 1, 0], [2, 4, 0]], find (1) a basis for the column space, (2) the null space solutions to Ax = 0, and (3) the rank. Then check consistency: decide whether each of the vectors b1 = (1,0,2) and b2 = (0,1,0) lies in the column space by solving Ax = b for each. Finally, verify your rank and nullity using rank(A) + nullity(A) = n where n is the number of columns.
steps: Compute the span of A’s columns and write a basis for the column space.
Solve Ax = 0 to describe the null space and choose a convenient basis for it.
Determine rank from the dimension of the column space and compute nullity from the dimension of the null space.
Check whether b1 and b2 are in the column space by testing consistency of Ax = b, and verify rank-nullity.

Student finds either the column space or the null space correctly but makes an error in the other one. slides.title: Roadmap for Week 9 Session 1
bullets: The column space of A is the span of its columns.
The null space of A is the set of solutions of Ax = 0.
slides.speakerNotes: Today connects “spans” to the column and null spaces, and then connects those spaces to rank via dimension.
slides.altText: Diagram-style roadmap showing three boxes labeled Column space, Null space, and Rank.

slides.title: Reminder: What makes a subspace?
bullets: A subspace contains the zero vector and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
The span of a set of vectors — all linear combinations — is always a subspace.
slides.speakerNotes: We will repeatedly use the fact that span is the smallest subspace containing the given vectors, and then apply it to matrix columns.
slides.altText: Checklist for subspace properties: contains 0, closed under addition, closed under scalar multiplication, and note that span always forms a subspace.

slides.title: Misconception check: lines and planes in R^3
bullets: A line or plane in R^3 is a subspace only if it passes through the origin.
If it does not contain the zero vector, it cannot be a subspace.
slides.speakerNotes: This is a common error when students picture geometric sets as subspaces without checking the zero vector and closure properties.
slides.altText: A line and a plane not passing through the origin are crossed out, while a line and plane through the origin are highlighted.

slides.title: Column space: definition and meaning
bullets: The column space of A is the span of its columns.
The column space consists of exactly those b for which Ax = b is consistent.
slides.speakerNotes: Interpretation: b is in the column space exactly when the linear system Ax = b has at least one solution.
slides.altText: Matrix A feeding into Ax=b, with the set of achievable outputs b shaded as the column space.

slides.title: Column space as a “smallest subspace”
bullets: The span of a set of vectors is the smallest subspace containing them.
Therefore, the column space is the smallest subspace that contains all columns of A.
slides.speakerNotes: This bridges the algebraic definition (span) with geometric/structural intuition (smallest subspace containing those vectors).
slides.altText: Growing subspaces around the columns until you reach the smallest one, labeled column space.

slides.title: Concrete worked example: column space via consistency
bullets: Let A = [[1, 2], [2, 4]]. Its columns are v1 = (1,2) and v2 = (2,4).
Any vector in the span has the form a v1 + b v2 = (a+2b, 2a+4b) = (t, 2t), so the column space is { (t, 2t) : t in R }.
slides.speakerNotes: Show a direct computation of span and then connect it to the equation Ax=b: Ax=b has solutions exactly when b has the form (t,2t).
slides.altText: Two proportional columns highlighted and the resulting column space shown as the line y=2x through the origin.

slides.title: Null space: definition and meaning
bullets: The null space of A is the set of solutions of Ax = 0.
The null space is a subspace of the domain.
slides.speakerNotes: Interpretation: vectors in the null space are inputs that get mapped to the zero vector by A.
slides.altText: Arrow diagram from vectors x through matrix A to the output Ax, with the ones mapping to 0 collected as the null space.

slides.title: Systems viewpoint: link to consistency
bullets: A linear system has exactly zero, one, or infinitely many solutions.
The system Ax = b is consistent when at least one solution exists.
slides.speakerNotes: This is the backbone for interpreting the column space: b is in the column space exactly when Ax=b is consistent.
slides.altText: Three cases for a linear system labeled: no solutions, one solution, infinitely many solutions, with “consistent” marking the first two.

slides.title: Rank and its dimension connection
bullets: The rank of A is the dimension of its column space.
The nullity is the dimension of its null space.
slides.speakerNotes: We now connect rank to the spaces we just defined, and prepare for the rank-nullity relationship.
slides.altText: Two dimensional boxes labeled Column space (dimension = rank) and Null space (dimension = nullity).

slides.title: Rank-nullity and invertibility
bullets: For an m-by-n matrix, rank(A) + nullity(A) = n, the number of columns of A.
A square n-by-n matrix is invertible exactly when its rank is n, equivalently when its nullity is 0.
slides.speakerNotes: Also keep the “rank counts pivots” intuition in mind, but we will stick to the kernel facts: dimension of column space and rank-nullity.
slides.altText: A formula card: rank(A)+nullity(A)=n, and a note: invertible iff rank = n iff nullity = 0.

slides.title: Misconception check: what rank does NOT count
bullets: Rank is not the number of nonzero entries or nonzero rows of the original matrix.
Rank is determined after row reduction via pivot columns, so proportional rows can force small rank.
slides.speakerNotes: This prevents the common “count nonzeros” strategy and redirects students to dimension/pivots after reduction.
slides.altText: Example illustration: matrix filled with nonzero entries but collapsing to rank 1 after reduction, with a “do not count nonzeros” sign.

body.text: Kickoff: what this week adds—how a linear transformation gets encoded by a matrix, and what matrix multiplication really does. Quick check: distinguish (1) solving linear systems via augmented matrices and row reduction vs (2) using matrices as operators.

Linear transformations ↔ matrices (conceptual bridge). Emphasize: a linear system has exactly zero, one, or infinitely many solutions—never exactly two—and systems can be represented as augmented matrices and solved by row reduction. Then preview how ‘the same data’ can be stored/processed using matrices.

Worked example (from systems to solution count): Show a tiny linear system that is inconsistent: x + y = 1 and x + y = 3. Explain that subtracting the equations gives 0 = -2, so there is no solution. Conclude: inconsistent systems have no solutions (and this matches the ‘zero, one, or infinitely many’ rule).

Matrix multiplication reality-check. In small groups, students compute one entry of AB using the definition: (i,j) entry is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. Then answer: does AB equal BA? They must justify using the condition about commutativity (generally not commutative; order matters).

Worked example reteach (walk-through): again use the same idea from the reading example name: ‘x + y = 1 and x + y = 3’ to reinforce the solution-count misconception. Start from the augmented-matrix viewpoint: write both equations, row-reduce, and show the contradiction row (something like 0x + 0y = -2). Conclude explicitly: this system is inconsistent, so it has zero solutions—this directly fixes the belief ‘Every system of equations has a solution.’

body.prompt: When you see a linear transformation written as y = T(x), what calculation do you want to reduce to a matrix multiplication, and why must you keep the order of factors when composing transformations?
body.tension: Students often treat matrices like numbers, but matrix multiplication is built from row–column dot products and is not generally commutative, so reversing multiplication changes the result or may break definedness.
followUps: Give an example of how you would compute T(x) once you have the matrix of T, using the dot-product description of entries.
Describe a situation where composing two transformation matrices would force you to preserve order, not swap them.
Explain how the dot-product rule for entries helps you debug a wrong matrix-vector computation.

body.task: Represent a linear transformation by a matrix and compute its effect on given input vectors. Then use matrix multiplication structure to check a composed transformation and explain what changes when you reverse the order of matrices. Finally, connect this back to linear systems by writing the augmented-matrix idea for solving unknowns in linear equations.
steps: Write down the matrix for a given linear rule by specifying how the rule acts on a general input vector in the chosen coordinate format.
Compute the output for at least two different input vectors by multiplying the matrix with the input as a column vector.
Given two transformation matrices, compute the composed effect using the matrix product in the correct order, and compare with the reversed order to determine whether it is different or undefined.
Briefly describe how a system of linear equations can be turned into an augmented matrix and solved by row reduction to find solutions.

body.q: Do we have to think of vectors as arrows in 2D or 3D to use linear transformations?
body.a: No. A vector space is defined by vector addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the axioms, and examples include polynomials, matrices, and functions under the usual operations.

body.q: Why is matrix multiplication not like multiplying numbers, and when is AB not defined?
body.a: AB is defined only when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B, and the (i,j) entry is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. Because matrix multiplication is generally not commutative, AB and BA can differ and the reverse product may be undefined.

body.text: Warm-up + goals: We’ll use the definition of eigenvectors/eigenvalues (Ax = λx) to (1) avoid common mistakes about the zero vector and zero eigenvalues, and (2) compute/recognize eigenvalues. Quick check: “What must an eigenvector be?” and “Can λ be 0?”

Eigenvalues & eigenvectors essentials: State the rule Ax = λx with x ≠ 0. Connect λ to the characteristic polynomial: λ is a root of det(A − λI). Then connect λ = 0 to invertibility: a zero eigenvalue means the matrix is not invertible (singular). Mention the independence facts we’ll use later (distinct eigenvalues → eigenvectors are automatically linearly independent).

Guided concept sorting (no computation yet): Students match short statements to categories: (i) eigenvector conditions (x ≠ 0, Ax parallel to x), (ii) eigenvalue meaning (λ from det(A − λI)), (iii) matrix property consequences (λ = 0 → singular), and (iv) vector-space reminders (what counts as a vector-space object). Instructor circulates and targets the misconceptions: “zero vector is always an eigenvector,” “zero eigenvalue means zero matrix,” and “eigenvectors are geometric arrows only.”

Worked example walkthrough (for students arriving cold): Example to work through: A = [[2,1],[1,2]]. Find eigenvalues by solving det(A − λI)=0, then find eigenvectors by solving (A − λI)x=0 for each λ. We’ll explicitly show why x must be nonzero even when Ax = λx holds (we ignore the trivial solution), and we’ll check the zero-eigenvalue case logic using the determinant/invertibility connection from the reading.

Reteach worked example (same example, but slower on the key pitfall): Using the same matrix A = [[2,1],[1,2]], redo the characteristic-polynomial step det(A − λI)=0 and then re-solve for eigenvectors. Pause for a misconception repair: “Eigenvectors are required to be nonzero — A0 = λ0 holds trivially and identifies nothing about the matrix.” Emphasize that when we solve (A − λI)x=0, we take nonzero solutions as eigenvectors; the zero solution is always present but never counts as an eigenvector.

body.markdown:
## Week 11 Study Guide: Eigenvalues & eigenvectors (plus key algebra reminders)

### Core definitions (must-know)
- **Eigenvector** of a square matrix **A**: a **nonzero** vector **x** such that **Ax = λx**. The scalar **λ** is the **eigenvalue**.
- **How to find eigenvalues**: **λ** is a root of the **characteristic polynomial** 
  \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\).

### Two misconception traps to watch
1) **Zero vector confusion**
- Wrong belief: “The zero vector is an eigenvector for every eigenvalue.”
- Repair: **Eigenvectors are required to be nonzero — A0 = λ0 holds trivially and identifies nothing about the matrix.**

2) **Zero eigenvalue confusion**
- Wrong belief: “A matrix with a zero eigenvalue is a zero matrix.”
- Repair: **A zero eigenvalue only means some nonzero vector is sent to zero — the matrix is singular, not necessarily zero.**

### Linear algebra reminders that matter in computations
- **Matrix multiplication**: **(i,j) entry of AB = (row i of A) · (column j of B)**, so it’s *not* entrywise like addition.
- **Order matters**: **AB = BA** only in special cases (e.g., one factor is the identity or both are powers of the same matrix).
- **Vectors vs geometry**: **Anything satisfying the vector-space axioms is a vector — polynomials, matrices, and functions included; geometry is one model, not the definition.**
- **Vector spaces and subsets**: A subset must contain the **zero vector** and be **closed under addition and scalar multiplication** (e.g., a line not through the origin fails).

### Self-check prompts
1) If **Ax = 0·x**, what does that say about **λ=0** and about invertibility?
2) When you solve **(A−λI)x=0**, which solution(s) count as eigenvectors, and why don’t we count the zero vector?
3) For matrix products, what operation creates each entry of **AB**: entrywise multiplication, or dot products of a row with a column?

### If you missed the reading
Eigenvalues/eigenvectors come from the condition **Ax = λx** with **x ≠ 0**. Eigenvalues are found by the characteristic polynomial **det(A − λI)=0**. A **zero eigenvalue** means the matrix is **singular** (not invertible), not that the whole matrix is the zero matrix. Eigenvectors are vectors in the vector-space sense: nonzero solutions to **(A−λI)x=0**, not geometric arrows-only objects.

body.prompt: Suppose a student claims that x = 0 is an eigenvector for every eigenvalue λ. Which part of the eigenvector definition stops that claim, and what does the equation A0 = λ0 actually tell you?
body.tension: The equation Ax = λx is true for x = 0 no matter what λ is, so students may wrongly think it proves eigenvalues/eigenvectors exist. The nonzero requirement is what makes the concept meaningful.
followUps: If λ = 0 is an eigenvalue, what does Ax = 0 tell you about the matrix’s behavior on some nonzero vector?
How does “distinct eigenvalues imply linearly independent eigenvectors” help you decide whether you have enough eigenvectors to diagonalize?

body.q: Can the zero vector be an eigenvector?
body.a: No. Eigenvectors must be nonzero, so x = 0 cannot be an eigenvector even though A0 = 0 is always true for any matrix A.

body.text: Start with the eigenvector/eigenvalue definition that drives diagonalization: for a square matrix A, an eigenvector is a nonzero vector x such that Ax = λx, and λ is an eigenvalue. Emphasize two gatekeeper facts before we talk about diagonalization: (1) eigenvectors must be nonzero, and (2) λ can be 0. Connect this directly to the characteristic polynomial det(A − λI): the eigenvalues are roots.

State the diagonalization criterion we will use repeatedly: an n×n matrix is diagonalizable exactly when it has n linearly independent eigenvectors. Add the helpful independence rule: eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are automatically linearly independent. Then show the “workflow” at a high level: find eigenvalues from det(A − λI), find eigenvectors for each eigenvalue, collect enough independent eigenvectors, and use them as the columns of P so that P^{-1}AP is diagonal.

Worked example (from the reading idea, walked carefully): Suppose det(A − λI) has two distinct eigenvalues λ1 and λ2, and for each eigenvalue you find an eigenvector (and therefore you have eigenspaces spanned by those eigenvectors). Because eigenvectors from distinct eigenvalues are automatically linearly independent, the two eigenvectors form a linearly independent set. For a 2×2 matrix, “n linearly independent eigenvectors” means you need exactly 2 independent eigenvectors, so A is diagonalizable. Next, build P using those eigenvectors as columns, and the diagonal entries become the corresponding eigenvalues in the same order as the columns. Finally, confirm the diagonalization statement P^{-1}AP = D by checking that AP = PD in column form: each eigenvector column v_i satisfies Av_i = λ_i v_i.

body.text: Orthogonality as “inner product = 0” (even when you can’t draw a picture): dot products of vectors, and the idea that orthogonal directions don’t interfere when we compute coordinates, distances, and projections. Use the kernel fact: nonzero orthogonal vectors are automatically linearly independent, and Gram–Schmidt converts any independent set into an orthogonal (or orthonormal) one spanning the same subspace.

Projections as linear operators: start with the projection test P is a projection iff P^2 = P. Then connect the decomposition v = Pv + (v − Pv): Pv lands in Im(P) and v − Pv lands in Ker(P). Emphasize the orthogonal-projection special case: only when P is orthogonal do we get Ker(P) = (Im(P))^⊥ and Im(P) = Ker(P)^⊥. Warn about oblique projections: if P^2=P but P^T≠P, those perpendicular relationships can fail.

WORKED EXAMPLE WALKTHROUGH (from today’s reading topic): Use orthogonal projections to interpret least squares geometrically. Follow the steps: (1) set up an inconsistent system Ax=b; (2) define the residual r = b − Ax̂; (3) use the least-squares fact that Ax̂ is the orthogonal projection of b onto Col(A); (4) conclude the residual is orthogonal to the column space, so normal equations AᵀAx̂ = Aᵀb arise. Then interpret what changes in data-fitting: Ax̂ is the closest point in Col(A), but it generally does not equal b.

RETEACH WORKED EXAMPLE: Re-walk the same least-squares geometric example step-by-step, this time focusing on the two common mistakes. First, address “Least squares finds an exact solution”: show that minimizing ||b−Ax|| means Ax̂ generally differs from b, because “being closest is not being equal.” Second, address “Best-fit line must pass through the data points”: explain that least squares minimizes the sum of squared vertical gaps, so it can miss every single data point. End by stating the projection view again: Ax̂ is the orthogonal projection of b onto the column space of A.

Quick transfer practice: students answer 6 short multiple-choice questions on (i) orthogonality (inner product vs pictures), (ii) deciding when perpendicular subspace relationships hold for projections, (iii) normal equations / orthogonal projection interpretation of least squares, and (iv) vector-space and linear-system sanity checks.

body.q: Is orthogonal just a picture idea (perpendicular lines)?
body.a: No. Orthogonality is defined by the dot product being zero, and that definition applies in any inner-product setting, including high-dimensional vectors or functions.

body.q: If P is a projection (P^2=P), is Im(P) always perpendicular to Ker(P)?

## Week 14 Comprehensive Review (what to be able to do)

### Key terms (quick definitions)
- **Linear system**: a collection of linear equations in the same variables; a **solution** makes every equation true simultaneously. A linear system has **exactly zero, one, or infinitely many solutions — never exactly two**.
- **Consistent / inconsistent**: consistent means at least one solution exists; inconsistent means no solution exists.
- **Row reduction / RREF**: using elementary row operations (swap, scale by nonzero, add multiple) to reach echelon/RREF; **elementary row operations do not change the solution set**. **Pivot positions are determined by echelon structure**, not by the size of entries.
- **Vector space**: closed under addition and scalar multiplication, contains a **zero vector**, and every vector has an **additive inverse**. Vector spaces need not be geometric arrows: **polynomials, matrices, and functions** are included.
- **Subspace**: must contain the zero vector and be closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
- **Span**: the smallest subspace containing given vectors; if vectors are parallel (or one is zero), the span collapses in dimension.
- **Rank**: dimension of the column space (number of pivot columns); **rank counts pivots after row reduction**.
- **Eigenvector/eigenvalue**: **Ax = λx with x nonzero**. A **zero eigenvalue** means the matrix is **not invertible**, not that the matrix must be zero.
- **Projection**: a linear operator P is a projection iff **P^2 = P**. For **orthogonal** projections, Im(P) and Ker(P) are perpendicular complements; for general projections (oblique), that perpendicular relationship need not hold.
- **Least squares**: if Ax=b has no exact solution, least squares finds x̂ minimizing the **residual length** ‖b − Ax‖, equivalently solving **AᵀAx̂ = Aᵀb**.

### Misconceptions to watch for (common exam traps)
1. Claim: **“Every system of equations has a solution.”** (False: contradictory equations like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 are inconsistent.)
2. Claim: **“Row operations change the solutions.”** (False: each elementary row operation is reversible and preserves the solution set.)
3. Claim: **“Vectors are always arrows in 2D or 3D.”** (False: anything satisfying vector-space axioms is a vector—polynomials, matrices, functions included.)
4. Claim: **“Matrix multiplication is entrywise, and AB = BA.”** (False: product AB uses row–column dot products and order matters.)
5. Claim: **“A nonzero matrix always has an inverse.”** (False: a square matrix with zero determinant can be nonzero yet not invertible.)
6. Claim: **“If the zero eigenvalue happens, the matrix is the zero matrix.”** (False: zero eigenvalue only means some nonzero vector is sent to zero.)
7. Claim: **“Any projection makes Im(P) perpendicular to Ker(P).”** (False unless P is an **orthogonal** projection.)
8. Claim: **“Least squares finds an exact solution.”** (False: it minimizes the residual; Ax̂ generally differs from b.)

### Self-check prompts (no calculators needed)
- If an augmented matrix reduces to a row like **[0 0 | 5]**, what does that tell you about the number of solutions?
- For a subset S of a vector space, can you point to: (i) the zero vector being in S, (ii) closure under addition, and (iii) closure under scalar multiplication?
- For a linear map given by a projection matrix P, does it satisfy **P^2 = P**? If yes, is it **orthogonal** (check symmetry) before concluding perpendicular relationships.

### If you missed the reading
This unit is a comprehensive review: you connect definitions to computational steps—especially how row reduction reveals consistency and pivot structure. You should be able to test subspace/vector space conditions quickly, without relying on geometry. Finally, you must use the correct matrix/projection/least-squares interpretations: products are row–column dot products, projections satisfy P^2=P, and least squares minimizes the residual rather than forcing exact equality.

## Week 3 (Session 1) Study Guide: Matrix algebra & matrix multiplication

### Key terms (know these precisely)
- **Matrix algebra**: operations on rectangular arrays. **Addition** and **scalar multiplication** act **entrywise**.
- **Matrix product AB**: defined only when **#columns of A = #rows of B**.
- **Dot product rule (definition of entries)**: the **(i, j) entry of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B**.
- **Non-commutativity**: generally **AB ≠ BA** and sometimes one product is **not even defined**.
- **Associativity & distributivity**: matrix multiplication **is associative** and **distributes over addition**, so algebra works **as long as factor order is preserved**.

### Misconceptions to watch for (common traps)
1. **“Matrix multiplication works entrywise, like addition.”** Correction: **AB combines rows of A with columns of B via dot products; the entrywise product is a different, rarely used operation.**
2. **“AB = BA for matrices, as with numbers.”** Correction: **Order matters in matrix products; AB = BA only in special cases, such as when one factor is the identity or both are powers of the same matrix.**

### Self-check prompts (do these before quizzes)
- If A is 2×3 and B is 4×2, is AB defined? Why?
- For a proposed (i,j) entry of AB, does it come from **row i of A with column j of B** (dot product)?
- Can you give one reason AB ≠ BA besides “it’s not commutative”? (Use either a dimension issue or a computed mismatch.)

### If you missed the reading
If you missed the reading, start by checking dimensions: AB is defined exactly when A’s number of columns matches B’s number of rows. Then compute AB using the rule that each (i,j) entry is a dot product of a row of A with a column of B. Do not use entrywise multiplication for the matrix product—addition is entrywise, but multiplication is row–column dot products. Finally, remember order matters: AB and BA can differ and may not both exist.

body.text: Start with what “inverse” actually means. For an n-by-n matrix A, say there is a matrix B such that AB = BA = I; then A is invertible and that B is the unique inverse A⁻¹. Emphasize: only square matrices can be invertible, and “having an inverse” is equivalent to “A has n pivots” / “det(A) ≠ 0” (use whichever framing students recall).

Connect invertibility to solving systems: if A is invertible, Ax = b has the unique solution x = A⁻¹b for every right-hand side b. Contrast with the failure case: if columns are linearly dependent, then A is not invertible (even if the matrix is not the zero matrix).

Worked example (from the reading goal for this week): Use the definition to test a candidate inverse. Let A be a square matrix and suppose someone claims B is the inverse. You check BOTH products: compute AB and BA and verify they equal the identity I. Then you can conclude A is invertible and the inverse is A⁻¹ = B; if either product is not I, the claim fails. During the check, watch for the common slip: assuming that because AB = I then automatically BA = I (in this course we require AB = BA = I in the definition).

Move to algebra with inverses and order. Derive/recall the key rule: the inverse of a product reverses order: (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹ (when both inverses exist). Stress that you do not get (AB)⁻¹ = A⁻¹B⁻¹; undoing two steps means you undo the last one first.

Quick transfer practice in pairs: (1) Decide invertible vs not invertible from a pivot/column-dependence statement, (2) choose the correct way to simplify an expression involving inverses, and (3) identify when a matrix product is defined. Collect answers and address the two headline misconceptions as they appear.

body.prompt: Take two invertible matrices A and B. If you first apply B and then apply A, what operation should undo the whole process, and why must the order reverse?
body.tension: Students often keep the same order when writing an inverse-of-product rule, but the definition requires undoing in the opposite sequence so that you get the identity.
followUps: Write expressions you would multiply to try to reach AB with an identity result.
What goes wrong if you try to use (AB)⁻¹ = A⁻¹B⁻¹ without checking order?
How does non-commutativity of matrix multiplication support the need for order reversal?

body.task: For each given square matrix, determine whether it is invertible. If it is invertible, compute its inverse by finding a matrix B such that AB = BA = I, and then use it to solve Ax=b for a specific right-hand side b. If it is not invertible, explain which invertibility criterion fails. Finally, verify your results by multiplying in the correct order.
steps: Check invertibility by determining whether the matrix has n pivots, using the pivot criterion given in class.
If invertible, propose an inverse B and verify AB = I and BA = I by computing the needed products.
Use the inverse to solve Ax=b by computing x = A⁻¹b.
Verify that your inverse-of-product rule respects order by checking a sample product of two matrices if the problem provides one.

rubricBands.observableBehavior: Student correctly states invertibility using AB = BA = I and checks the criterion using n pivots (or equivalent nonzero determinant reasoning) on a square matrix example.
Student identifies that invertibility matters only for square matrices and attempts to find an inverse, but may verify only one side (AB = I or BA = I) or makes a minor arithmetic/product-order slip.
Student claims that every nonzero matrix has an inverse, or uses (AB)⁻¹ = A⁻¹B⁻¹ without reversing the order.

body.q: Why do we need both AB = I and BA = I in the definition of inverse?
body.a: Because the inverse is defined as a two-sided undoing: B must undo A when multiplied on the left and on the right, giving the identity in both products. This is exactly what the condition AB = BA = I encodes.

body.q: When can we use (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹?
body.a: You use (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹ only when both inverses exist. The order reverses because the composed action AB must be undone in the opposite sequence to return to the identity.

body.text: Warm-up on what determinants are: scalar from a square matrix; det ≠ 0 exactly when the matrix is invertible; geometrically, |det| scales area/volume. Then connect determinant to solving Ax=b via invertibility (unique solution exists for every b when det(A)≠0).

Worked example: determinant of a product. Start with “det(AB) = det(A)det(B)” and walk through the full computation workflow: (a) compute det(A); (b) compute det(B); (c) multiply the results to get det(AB). Then interpret: if det(A)=0 or det(B)=0, det(AB)=0 so AB is not invertible. Finish by checking consistency with the invertibility rule: a matrix is invertible iff its determinant is nonzero.

Mini-application stations (no new theory): 3 short prompts where students must (i) choose between multiplicative vs additive determinant behavior, (ii) infer invertibility from determinant, and (iii) predict how row operations change det (sign / scaling / unchanged). Students justify with the exact property name or rule.

Reteach worked example (same idea, different numbers): determinant sign and zero via row operations. I’ll work through an explicit row-operation chain: start from a matrix where we can swap rows, then scale a row, then add a multiple of another row so we reach a simpler form. At each step, apply the rule: swapping rows flips the sign; scaling a row scales the determinant; adding a multiple of one row to another leaves it unchanged. Conclude det is 0 when the row operations force dependence (e.g., create equal rows), matching the invertibility criterion.

body.prompt: When you do row reduction to compute a determinant, how would you decide whether the determinant changes sign, scales, or stays the same after each row operation?
body.tension: Students often try to apply one determinant rule (like “it changes when rows change”) too broadly, which can lead them to treat det(A+B) like det(A) + det(B) or to think entry size controls det.
followUps: What specific row operation corresponds to a sign flip, and why?
If you scale a row by k, what happens to the determinant?
If you add a multiple of one row to another, what happens to the determinant?

body.task: Compute determinants of two 2×2 matrices using row operations and the determinant-change rules. For each matrix, write down which row operations you used and state how the determinant changed (sign flip, scaling, or unchanged). Finally, determine whether each matrix is invertible using the criterion that a square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero.
steps: Choose a 2×2 matrix that is not already triangular and plan row operations to create a zero in the lower-left entry.
Perform the row operations carefully, and record how each operation affects the determinant.
Compute the final determinant from the resulting matrix.
Decide invertibility by checking whether the determinant is nonzero.

rubricBands.observableBehavior: Uses the row-operation determinant rules correctly and obtains the correct determinant value for each matrix.
Performs row operations mostly correctly but makes a consistent mistake about how one type of row operation affects the determinant.
Confuses additive behavior with multiplicative behavior by trying to relate determinants of sums to sums of determinants, or incorrectly ties determinant size to entry size.

body.q: If I swap two rows, does the determinant become the negative of the original?
body.a: Yes. Swapping rows flips the sign of the determinant.

body.text: Start with the definition: what it takes to be a vector space. Emphasize the two “musts” (zero vector + additive inverses) and the closure conditions. Contrast R^n as an example with other vector spaces (polynomials, matrices, functions) so students don’t equate “vector” with “arrow in 2D/3D.”

Subspaces: build the checklist. A subspace is a subset that contains the zero vector AND is closed under addition AND scalar multiplication. Then connect the idea of span: linear combinations of given vectors always form a subspace, and the span is the smallest subspace containing them.

Worked example (from this week’s core idea): take S = span{(1,2,0), (1,2,3)} in R^3. Compute a general linear combination a(1,2,0)+b(1,2,3) = (a+b, 2a+2b, 3b). Describe S as the set of all vectors of that form and explicitly note it contains the zero vector (choose a=b=0) and is closed under addition and scaling (because adding/scaling combinations stays a combination).

Quick subspace-sorting: students decide whether each candidate is a subspace, then justify using the three checks (zero vector, closed under addition, closed under scalar multiplication). Include one “trap” case: a line/plane not through the origin; and one “trap” case: a set not closed under addition or scaling.

Reteach the worked example above (S = span{(1,2,0), (1,2,3)}): re-derive the parameterization (a+b, 2a+2b, 3b) and then do the subspace checklist on it. Show closure explicitly: if u=(a+b,2a+2b,3b) and v=(c+d,2c+2d,3d), then u+v corresponds to choosing (a+c, b+d). Also show that scaling by k just scales the parameters, so k·u is still in S.

body.prompt: Pick a subset S of R^2 and explain which vector-space or subspace test fails: does S contain the zero vector, is it closed under addition, and is it closed under scalar multiplication?
body.tension: Students often assume geometry alone decides whether something is a subspace, but the axioms and closure conditions do the deciding.
followUps: If S is a line not through the origin, which of the subspace conditions fails first?
If S is the span of two vectors, what changes when the vectors are parallel?
How do you use the definition of span to guarantee you get a subspace?

body.task: For each set below, decide whether it is a subspace of the stated vector space. Justify your answer using the required conditions: it must contain the zero vector and be closed under addition and scalar multiplication. Then, for the sets that are not subspaces, state exactly which condition fails. Your work should be explicit, not just a guess.
steps: Check whether the set contains the zero vector stated by the ambient vector space.
Test closure under addition using two generic elements from the set (or an example pair).
Test closure under scalar multiplication using a generic scalar and a generic element from the set.
If the set is not a subspace, name the specific failing condition.

rubricBands.observableBehavior: Student applies the subspace definition by checking zero inclusion and both closure properties, and the justification matches the conditions using a concrete test.
Student identifies some correct conditions but does not perform a clear closure test or gives an argument that does not specify how addition or scaling stays inside the set.
Student claims that any line or plane in R^3 is a subspace, or that the span of two vectors is always a plane, without checking the missing zero vector or the collapse when vectors are parallel.

body.q: Is every set of vectors a vector space?
body.a: No. A vector space is a set with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the axioms, including that it contains the zero vector and that it is closed under addition and scaling.

body.q: Why is the span automatically a subspace?
body.a: The span is defined as all linear combinations of the given vectors, and taking sums and scalar multiples of linear combinations keeps you in the same form. Therefore the span contains the zero vector and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

body.text: Warm-up + definitions. Write the condition for independence: a set is linearly independent when the only way to make the zero vector is using all zero coefficients; otherwise there is a dependence relation. Emphasize: dependence is about redundancy (one vector can be written as a linear combination of the others). Quick check: show that a set containing the zero vector is automatically dependent.

Independence via solving: connect to matrices. State the column viewpoint: the columns of A are independent exactly when Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution (every column is a pivot column). Then use this to interpret what it means for columns to be dependent. Transition to spans/bases: a basis is both independent and spanning; coordinates are the unique linear combination of basis vectors.

Worked example: independence vs “different vectors.” Use the reading’s misconception example and resolve it directly. Consider v1=(1,0), v2=(0,1), v3=(1,1). They are pairwise different, but v3 = v1 + v2, so there is a nontrivial linear combination giving the zero vector: (1)v1 + (1)v2 + (-1)v3 = 0. Therefore {v1,v2,v3} is linearly dependent, showing that independence is about redundancy, not distinctness.

Mini-lab stations (small groups). Station A: decide dependent/independent for short sets in R^2 and justify with a dependence relation or by describing why the only zero combination is trivial. Station B: given a candidate set, check whether it could be a basis by verifying both spanning and independence. Station C: compute/compare dimension using the rule “basis vectors count; dimension is the common size of any basis.” Groups must cite the specific criterion they used.

Reteach worked example (walk-through again, same example to solidify). Re-derive v3=(1,1) from v1=(1,0) and v2=(0,1): since (1,0)+(0,1)=(1,1), the set {v1,v2,v3} has a dependence relation. Then restate the independence test in the exact form: independence would require that the only linear combination equaling the zero vector uses all zero coefficients; but here we have a nontrivial combination that gives zero, so it’s dependent.

body.prompt: Take the example v1=(1,0), v2=(0,1), v3=(1,1) in R^2. Is the set {v1,v2,v3} independent or dependent, and which definition would you use to justify your answer? Then decide what a basis could be and what the dimension must be.
body.tension: Students often think “independent just means all vectors are different,” so they mislabel sets like (1,0), (0,1), (1,1). The real criterion is redundancy via a zero-producing linear combination or equivalently one vector being a linear combination of the others.
followUps: Find a smallest subset of these vectors that is a basis for R^2.
Explain how you would detect dependence using Ax=0 without explicitly solving for coordinates.

body.task: For each of the following sets in R^2 or R^3, determine whether the set is linearly independent, and justify using the definition (zero combination) or the dependence criterion (one vector is a combination of the others). Then, when you decide a set is independent and has the right size, state whether it is a basis and give the dimension of the space you are working in. Finally, for at least one vector, write its coordinates as a unique linear combination of basis vectors.
steps: For each set, decide dependent or independent using either the “only trivial combination gives zero” definition or “some vector is a linear combination of the others.”
For the sets you identify as independent with the correct number of vectors in R^n, conclude they form a basis and state the dimension.
For one chosen basis, express one vector from the space as its unique linear combination and report the coordinates.
Check your work by confirming spanning when you claim a basis and confirm the dependence relation when you claim dependence.

rubricBands.observableBehavior: The student applies the definition of linear independence with an explicit linear combination or an explicit dependence relation, and then uses the basis definition (independent and spanning) to conclude basis status. The student states the correct dimension and provides correct coordinates as a unique linear combination.

The student identifies linear dependence or independence correctly in most cases, but the justification is incomplete (for example, they claim dependence without exhibiting the linear combination). The student may identify a basis but cannot reliably explain why spanning or uniqueness holds.

The student equates independence with vectors being different, or treats “more vectors” as meaning “more independent.” The student also confuses dimension with the number of vectors listed rather than the size of a basis.

slides.title: Where we are heading this week
bullets: We will decide when vectors are linearly independent.
We will use independence and spanning to build bases.
We will translate “number of basis vectors” into the dimension of a vector space.
slides.speakerNotes: This is the bridge from the earlier discussion of vector spaces and subspaces into the core toolkit: independence, basis, and dimension. Keep the checklist mindset: independence tells us about redundancy, spanning tells us about coverage, and dimension tells us the size of a basis.
slides.altText: Three goals for the lesson: linear independence, basis, and dimension.

slides.title: Linear independence: the definition
bullets: A set of vectors is linearly independent when the only linear combination that equals the zero vector uses all zero coefficients.
A nontrivial combination that equals the zero vector is a dependence relation.
slides.speakerNotes: Emphasize “only the zero-coefficient combination gives zero.” If we find even one nontrivial combination that hits zero, independence fails.
slides.altText: Definition of linear independence via linear combinations equaling the zero vector.

slides.title: Zero vector and dependence
bullets: A set containing the zero vector is automatically linearly dependent.
A set of vectors is dependent exactly when some vector in it is a linear combination of the others.
slides.speakerNotes: This gives two quick dependence tests. The zero vector kills independence immediately, and more generally dependence means redundancy: one vector can be rebuilt from the rest.
slides.altText: Zero vector implies dependence; dependence corresponds to one vector being a combination of the others.

slides.title: Independence via matrices (pivot idea)
bullets: The columns of a matrix A are independent exactly when Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution.
That means every column is a pivot column.
slides.speakerNotes: This connects the vector definition to the matrix viewpoint. You can treat Ax=0 as asking whether there is any nontrivial linear combination of the columns that gives zero.
slides.altText: Columns are independent exactly when Ax=0 has only the trivial solution, meaning pivot columns.

slides.title: Worked example: test independence directly
bullets: We have v3 = v1 + v2, so {v1,v2,v3} is linearly dependent.
slides.speakerNotes: Show the actual dependence relation: (1,0)+(0,1)=(1,1). This also illustrates that pairwise different vectors can still be dependent.
slides.altText: Example in R^2 showing v3 equals v1 plus v2, so the set is dependent.

slides.title: Basis: independent plus spanning
bullets: A basis is a linearly independent set that spans the space.
Every basis of a given space has the same number of vectors, and that count is the space's dimension.
slides.speakerNotes: State the two conditions as a single recipe: independence removes redundancy, spanning ensures every vector can be built from the basis.
slides.altText: Basis defined as independent and spanning; all bases have the same size, equal to dimension.

slides.title: Coordinates with a basis
bullets: Every vector in the space is a unique linear combination of basis vectors.
The coefficients in that combination are the vector’s coordinates in that basis.
slides.speakerNotes: Uniqueness is important: if you had two different coefficient sets, you would contradict linear independence. This uniqueness is what makes “coordinates” well-defined.
slides.altText: Uniqueness of coordinates relative to a basis.

slides.title: Basis and dimension in R^n (useful rule)
bullets: In R^n, any n independent vectors form a basis.
In R^n, any spanning set of n vectors is automatically independent.
slides.speakerNotes: These are practical shortcuts for building bases and deciding dimension in finite-dimensional spaces.
slides.altText: Rule: n independent vectors in R^n form a basis; n spanning vectors are independent.

slides.title: Dimension is not “how many vectors you have”
bullets: Dimension counts basis vectors, not members of the space.
In R^2 there are infinitely many vectors, but the dimension is 2.
slides.speakerNotes: Reinforce two common confusions: (1) dimension is about basis size, not the total number of vectors; (2) a space can have infinitely many different bases, but they all have the same size.
slides.altText: Dimension counts basis size; R^2 has dimension 2 even though it has infinitely many vectors.

slides.title: Tie-in to vector spaces and subspaces
bullets: A vector space is a set with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the vector-space axioms; R^n is the standard example.
A subspace contains the zero vector and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication; spans are always subspaces.
slides.speakerNotes: This slide connects the definitions you already know: we talk about bases and dimension inside vector spaces, and we form subspaces using spans. Those spans then inherit the vector-space structure.
slides.altText: Vector spaces satisfy axioms; subspaces contain zero and are closed; spans form subspaces.

body.text: Midterm overview: how systems, row reduction, and subspaces connect. Focus checklist: (1) A system has 0, 1, or infinitely many solutions (not exactly two). (2) Convert to an augmented matrix and solve by row reduction. (3) What consistency means. (4) Subspaces: must contain the zero vector and be closed under addition and scalar multiplication; span is the smallest subspace containing a set.

assets.conceptName: midterm exam covering systems through subspaces

body.text: Quick concept sort (no calculators): Students classify 8 statements as True/False: inconsistent vs consistent; 'two solutions implies infinitely many'; span of parallel vectors; line/plane through origin vs not; subspace closure; vectors as arrows vs general vectors; and basics of matrix multiplication order. Students then justify each with 1 phrase: 'misses zero' / 'not closed' / 'parallel lines' / 'line of solutions' / 'dot products rows with columns' / etc.

assets.conceptName: midterm exam covering systems through subspaces

body.text: Worked example: Determining consistency by contradiction. Consider the system x + y = 1 and x + y = 3. Subtract the equations to get 0 = -2, which is impossible. Therefore the system has no solutions (inconsistent). Emphasize the core pattern: two equations can represent parallel lines that never meet, so 'no solution' is the correct outcome.

assets.conceptName: midterm exam covering systems through subspaces

body.text: Reteach (worked example): Two solutions ⇒ infinitely many (using a 'line through two solutions' argument). Take a system that has two distinct solutions (e.g., solutions at (x,y) = (1,0) and (x,y) = (0,1) for some consistent linear system). Explain: once two distinct solutions exist, the set of all convex combinations (1−t)u + t v (for real t) also solves the system because the equations are linear. This is why 'over the real numbers, once a linear system has two distinct solutions it has infinitely many'—the whole line through the two solutions solves the system.

assets.conceptName: midterm exam covering systems through subspaces

body.text: Bridge to subspaces and subspace pictures for the exam. (1) Span(V) is always a subspace and is the smallest one containing V. (2) Span of two vectors: if independent, you get a plane; if parallel (or one is zero), the span collapses to a line or point. (3) Subspace test: zero vector + closure under addition/scalar multiplication. Close with what column space and null space represent at the level needed for the midterm: column space corresponds to consistent Ax=b, and null space is solutions to Ax=0 and is a subspace.

assets.conceptName: midterm exam covering systems through subspaces

body.prompt: Midterm-style: For a given matrix A, explain how you would recognize which right-hand sides b make Ax = b consistent, using the idea of column space membership.
body.tension: Students often treat consistency as something you guess from the equations, but the midterm expects you to translate it into a subspace/span statement.
followUps: When you solve Ax = 0, what subspace do you get and what is it called?
Why does row reduction preserve the solution set even though the matrix changes?
In a span argument, what does “smallest subspace containing them” mean operationally?

assets.conceptName: midterm exam covering systems through subspaces

body.task: Take a set of vectors S and (i) compute span(S) in a concrete example, then (ii) use the definition of subspace to justify whether a candidate set is a subspace or not. Next, write a short explanation connecting a linear system Ax = b to the column space statement about consistency, and connect Ax = 0 to the null space statement. Your work should show the key membership logic, not just the final verdicts.
steps: Choose two vectors in R^2 or R^3 and compute all linear combinations explicitly to describe span(S).
Propose a candidate subset T and test it against the subspace requirements for containing zero and closure under addition and scalar multiplication.
Pick a small matrix A and explain which b make Ax = b consistent using the column space characterization.
State what the null space of A is for your same matrix A by describing the solutions to Ax = 0.

rubricBands.observableBehavior: Student applies the definition of subspace and gives an explicit span computation that produces the smallest subspace containing the given vectors.
Student uses span or subspace language but makes a partial justification, such as checking only one closure property or describing the set without fully showing the linear combinations.
Student claims that any line or plane in R^3 is a subspace, or claims that span of two vectors is always a plane, regardless of dependence.

body.q: Is the span of two vectors always a plane in R^3?
body.a: No. If the two vectors are parallel (or one is zero), their span collapses to a line or a point; the span’s dimension depends on independence.

body.q: Does every linear system have at least one solution?
body.a: No. Some systems are inconsistent, such as x + y = 1 and x + y = 3, which have zero solutions.

body.text: Warm-up and map the day: We’re connecting three ideas—(1) column space (what right-hand sides b make Ax=b consistent), (2) null space (solutions of Ax=0), and (3) rank (dimension of the column space, i.e., number of pivot columns). We’ll keep one rule in mind: span is always the smallest subspace containing the given vectors.

Subspaces and spans first: review the subspace test (contains 0; closed under addition and scalar multiplication). Then connect it to the geometric misconceptions: “Any line or plane in R^3 is a subspace” is false unless it passes through the origin; and “The span of two vectors is always a plane” is false when the vectors are parallel (or one is zero), because the span collapses to a line/point.

Worked example walkthrough (from the reading’s core pattern): Find column space, null space, and rank for the matrix A = [[1,0],[0,0]]. We interpret the column space as the span of the columns: col1=(1,0), col2=(0,0) so Col(A)=span{(1,0)}. Next solve Ax=b for consistency to describe Col(A) as exactly the b’s that work: Ax=(x1,0), so Ax=b is consistent exactly when b=(b1,0). For the null space solve Ax=0: (x1,0)=(0,0) so x1=0 and x2 is free; thus Null(A)={ (0,t) : t in R }, a 1D subspace. Finally rank is dim(Col(A)) which is 1; equivalently, row reduction shows one pivot column.

Guided practice rotations: small groups get 2–3 short prompts where they (a) decide whether a given geometric set is a subspace, (b) determine whether a vector b is in the column space by checking consistency, and (c) compute nullity/rank quickly from Ax=0 and pivot counts. Students must explicitly justify using ‘Ax=b is consistent’ for column space and ‘Ax=0’ for null space.

Reteach the worked example logic (using the same example A = [[1,0],[0,0]]): (1) Column space: “Col(A) is the span of its columns” → span{(1,0)} → all vectors of the form (c,0). (2) Null space: solve Ax=0 → x1=0, x2 free → line through the origin in the domain. (3) Rank: dimension of the column space → rank=1. Then explicitly fix common mistakes: rank is not “#nonzero entries,” and not every line/plane is a subspace unless it contains the zero vector and is scaling-closed.

body.prompt: For a given matrix A, how would you decide whether a particular vector b is in the column space using only the equation Ax=b? Then, how would you decide whether a particular vector x is in the null space using only Ax=0?
body.tension: Students often treat column space and null space as geometric objects to guess, but the definitions tie them exactly to solvability and homogeneous solutions.
followUps: Pick a specific A and b, and argue “b is (or is not) in Col(A)” by stating what Ax=b does.
Pick a specific A and x, and argue “x is (or is not) in Null(A)” by checking Ax=0.
Relate your conclusions to rank by stating how many independent directions you see in Col(A).

body.q: Is the column space always a subspace?
body.a: Yes. The column space is the span of the columns of A, and a span is always a subspace.

body.q: If Ax=b has a solution, is that b automatically in the null space?
body.a: No. The null space is the set of x that satisfy Ax=0, while the column space is the set of b values for which Ax=b is consistent.

body.text: Hook + goal: In this week’s reading we connect “linear transformations” to “their matrices.” We’ll translate a rule that takes a vector x to an output T(x) into a matrix A, and we’ll use matrix multiplication properties carefully (especially dimensions and order).

Representing a transformation with a matrix: Start from the idea that a linear transformation is determined by what it does to basis vectors; that gives a matrix (the matrix of the transformation). Then interpret the product A x as “the transformation applied to x” in coordinates. Emphasize: matrix multiplication AB is defined only when the columns of A match the rows of B, and (i,j) entry of AB is row i of A dotted with column j of B.

Worked example (walk-through): Build the matrix of a transformation from its action on vectors in coordinates. Use the reading’s example: “Let T(x,y) = (x+2y, 3y). Find the matrix A such that T(x,y) = A [x;y].” Compute A by matching coefficients: T(x,y) = (1·x + 2·y, 0·x + 3·y) so A = [[1,2],[0,3]]. Then verify by multiplying A [x;y].

Reteach worked example (same example, extra slowness): Take T(x,y) = (x+2y, 3y) and again construct A from the coefficient pattern. Re-do the check explicitly: A [x;y] = [[1,2],[0,3]] [x;y] = [(1)x + (2)y, (0)x + (3)y] = (x+2y, 3y). Tie back to the key interpretation: once you have A, composing transformations corresponds to multiplying their matrices (with factor order preserved).

Mini-practice + misconception sweep: 6 quick prompts (no full solutions): (1) Decide if a matrix product is defined (dimensions). (2) Decide whether AB=BA should hold. (3) Identify the (i,j) entry of AB as a dot product. (4) For transformations, plug a test vector to confirm the matrix you found. (5) Quick vector-space check on a subset. (6) Linear-system consistency check: 0/1/infinitely many solutions (never exactly two).

body.markdown:
### Linear transformations → matrices (week 10)

**Key terms / definitions**
- **Linear system (consistency):** a collection of linear equations in the same variables. It has **exactly zero, one, or infinitely many solutions—never exactly two**. **Consistent** means at least one solution exists; **inconsistent** means no solution exists.
- **Linear transformation:** a rule T that takes vectors to vectors and behaves linearly (so it can be represented by a matrix in coordinates).
- **Matrix of a transformation:** the matrix A that makes the coordinate relation **T(x)=A x** true.
- **Matrix product AB:** defined only when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B. The **(i,j) entry of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B**.
- **Order matters:** matrix multiplication is generally **not commutative**; AB and BA can differ or one product may be undefined.

**Misconceptions to watch for**
- “**Every system of equations has a solution.**” (Reality: some systems are **inconsistent**.)
- “**If a system has more than one solution, it has some finite number of them.**” (Reality: over the reals, two distinct solutions imply **infinitely many**.)
- “**Matrix multiplication works entrywise, like addition.**” (Reality: AB uses **dot products** of rows with columns.)
- “**AB = BA for matrices, as with numbers.**” (Reality: **order matters**; AB=BA only in special cases.)
- “**Vectors are always arrows in 2D or 3D space.**” (Reality: vectors can be **polynomials, matrices, functions**, etc.; geometry is a model, not the definition.)
- “**Any subset of R^n is a vector space.**” (Reality: a subset must contain the **zero vector** and be **closed under addition and scalar multiplication**.)

**Self-check prompts**
1. If you find two distinct solutions to a real linear system, how many solutions are there total?
2. For a product AB, what object gives the (i,j) entry: row–column dot product or entrywise multiplication?
3. Does matrix multiplication commute? If not, when can AB=BA happen?

### If you missed the reading
If the goal is “represent a linear transformation with a matrix,” you should be able to take a coordinate formula for T(x) and turn it into a matrix A so that **T(x)=A x**. When verifying your A, always test with a specific input vector and re-compute the product. Also remember the basics of matrix multiplication: **(i,j) of AB is a dot product of row i of A with column j of B**, and **order matters**.

body.text: Goal for today: recognize eigenvectors/eigenvalues and use the definition to compute them. Start from the definition: for a square matrix A, an eigenvector x satisfies Ax = λx, with x required to be nonzero; λ is the eigenvalue. Emphasize: λ comes from solving det(A − λI) = 0 (characteristic polynomial).

Worked example (Eigenvalues from det(A − λI)): Let A = [[2,0],[0,3]]. Compute det(A − λI) = det([[2−λ,0],[0,3−λ]]) = (2−λ)(3−λ). So the eigenvalues are λ = 2 and λ = 3. Then find eigenvectors by solving (A−2I)x=0 and (A−3I)x=0.

Turn eigenvalues into eigenvectors and connect to vector-space thinking. For λ = 2: (A−2I) = [[0,0],[0,1]], so x must satisfy second component = 0, giving eigenvectors of the form (t,0). For λ = 3: (A−3I) = [[−1,0],[0,0]], so first component = 0, giving eigenvectors of the form (0,t). Mention distinct eigenvalues → eigenvectors are automatically linearly independent. Also underline two common traps: (1) eigenvectors must be nonzero (A0 = λ0 holds but tells you nothing), and (2) a zero eigenvalue indicates singularity (some nonzero vector maps to 0), not that A is the zero matrix.

Quick application stations: (a) decide whether a given nonzero vector is an eigenvector for a given λ, (b) compute which λ values make a given equation Ax = λx possible, (c) practice spotting correct vs incorrect statements about zero eigenvalues and about matrix multiplication order/dot-products.

Reteach with the same worked example: Use A = [[2,0],[0,3]] again. Walk through the corrective checks: Why x must be nonzero in Ax = λx (the zero vector makes Ax = λx true for any λ, so it doesn’t identify eigenvalues/eigenvectors). Also show the meaning of a zero eigenvalue using the same logic (if λ = 0 were an eigenvalue, then (A−0I)x=Ax=0 would have a nonzero solution, meaning A is not invertible). Keep the order-of-operations idea straight: the product AB uses dot products of rows with columns, not entrywise multiplication.

body.markdown:
## Week 11 Study Guide: Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors

### Core definitions (what to use on homework)
- **Eigenvector/eigenvalue**: For a square matrix **A**, a vector **x** is an **eigenvector** if **x ≠ 0** and **Ax = λx**. The scalar **λ** is the **eigenvalue**.
- **How to find λ**: Solve **det(A − λI) = 0** (characteristic polynomial roots).
- **Zero eigenvalue meaning**: A **zero eigenvalue** means there exists a **nonzero** x such that **Ax = 0**. That makes **A singular** (not invertible).
- **Distinct eigenvalues**: Eigenvectors from **distinct eigenvalues** are **automatically linearly independent**.

### Must-remember misconceptions to watch for
1. **“The zero vector is an eigenvector for every eigenvalue.”** False because **eigenvectors are required to be nonzero**; **A0 = λ0** holds trivially and gives no information.
2. **“A matrix with a zero eigenvalue is a zero matrix.”** False; a zero eigenvalue only guarantees **some nonzero** vector maps to **0**. The matrix is **singular, not necessarily zero**.
3. **Matrix product confusion**: **AB** is defined by **dot products of rows of A with columns of B**, not entrywise multiplication, and **order matters** (generally **AB ≠ BA**).
4. **Vector definition confusion**: Geometry arrows are one model, but **any object satisfying the vector-space axioms is a vector** (polynomials, matrices, functions included).

### Self-check prompts
- If someone claims “x = 0 is an eigenvector for λ,” what exact requirement about eigenvectors do you invoke?
- If you find an eigenvalue λ = 0, which property must follow (invertible or not?), and why must the vector witnessing it be **nonzero**?
- For a matrix product **AB**, which pieces are paired to form the entry (row i of A with column j of B)?

### If you missed the reading
Eigenvalues/eigenvectors are built directly from the equation **Ax = λx** with the requirement that **x is nonzero**. The value **λ** comes from the characteristic polynomial **det(A − λI)**. A **zero eigenvalue** means there is a **nonzero** vector that gets sent to **0**, so the matrix is **singular**, not necessarily the zero matrix. Finally, remember vector-space ideas and basic matrix multiplication rules so you don’t mix up “entrywise” operations with true matrix products.

body.a: Eigenvectors must be nonzero by definition, but the eigenvalue λ can be zero; a zero eigenvalue means the matrix is not invertible.

body.markdown:
## Diagonalization quick guide (Week 12)

**Eigenvector / eigenvalue.** For a square matrix **A**, a **(nonzero)** vector **x** is an **eigenvector** if **Ax = λx**. The number **λ** is the **eigenvalue**. To find λ, solve the characteristic equation: **det(A − λI) = 0**.

**Zero vs nonzero.** 
- **Eigenvectors must be nonzero.** Even though **A0 = λ0** is always true, **that does not make the zero vector an eigenvector**.
- **An eigenvalue can be zero.** A **zero eigenvalue** means **there exists a nonzero x with Ax = 0**, so **A is not invertible (singular)**—the matrix is **not necessarily** the zero matrix.

**Diagonalizable.** An **n-by-n** matrix is diagonalizable **exactly when** it has **n linearly independent eigenvectors**. Also, eigenvectors corresponding to **distinct eigenvalues** are **automatically linearly independent**.

### Misconceptions to watch for
1) “The zero vector is an eigenvector for every eigenvalue.” (No: eigenvectors must be nonzero.)
2) “If an eigenvalue is 0, then A must be the zero matrix.” (No: 0 eigenvalue just means A is singular.)

### Self-check prompts
- If your eigen-solution set for (A − λI)x = 0 includes x = 0 and some nonzero vectors, which ones count as eigenvectors?
- If λ = 0 is an eigenvalue, what does Ax = 0 tell you about invertibility?
- To claim diagonalization for an n-by-n matrix, what must you have besides eigenvalues?

### If you missed the reading
Re-center on the definition: eigenvectors satisfy **Ax = λx** and must be **nonzero**. Then diagonalization is not automatic—you need **n linearly independent eigenvectors** for an n-by-n matrix. If you find a **zero eigenvalue**, interpret it as: some **nonzero** vector is sent to **zero** by A, so A is **singular**, not necessarily the zero matrix. Finally, diagonalize by assembling P from eigenvectors and D from eigenvalues only when you truly have enough independent eigenvectors.

If diagonalization is not possible, clearly state which part of the diagonalization criterion fails.

slides.title: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues (definition)
bullets: An eigenvector of a square matrix A is a nonzero vector x with Ax = λx.
The scalar λ is the eigenvalue and it comes from solving det(A − λI) = 0.
slides.speakerNotes: Emphasize the nonzero requirement for eigenvectors, and that eigenvalues are found from the characteristic polynomial.

slides.title: A test for when diagonalization works

body.text: Warm-up: define orthogonality by the dot product (inner product) being zero. Emphasize that this is a condition on vectors (or functions), not a “looks perpendicular in a picture” rule. Quick payoff: orthogonal directions make coordinates/projections/distance calculations cleaner because directions don’t interfere.

Projections: start from the projection operator facts. A linear operator P is a projection iff P^2 = P. Then use the decomposition v = Pv + (v − Pv), with Pv in Im(P) and (v − Pv) in Ker(P). Stress the orthogonal-vs-oblique distinction: only orthogonal projections force Im(P) ⟂ Ker(P).

Worked example (no reading required): Let A = [[1],[1]] (so A maps x to x·(1,1) in R^2). Given b = (2,0), find the least-squares solution x̂ by projection: compute Ax̂ = Proj_{Col(A)}(b). The column space is span{(1,1)}. The projection of b onto span{(1,1)} is ( (b·u)/(u·u) )u with u=(1,1). Then Ax̂ = ((b·u)/(u·u))u = ((2)/(2))(1,1) = (1,1), so x̂ = 1. Conclude: least squares does not require Ax̂ = b; it finds the point in the column space closest to b (minimizing residual length).

Mini-application set (pairs): 3 multiple-choice style prompts (orthogonality definition, orthogonal vs general projection relationship between Im(P) and Ker(P), and interpreting least squares as minimizing residual). Students must justify their choice in 1 sentence referencing the correct condition (dot product zero / P^T=P for orthogonal projection / residual minimization). Instructor circulates and collects the top confusion themes.

Reteach the same worked example: replay the projection-based least-squares idea for b = (2,0) onto span{(1,1)}. Walk through how we know this is a projection (closest point in the column space) and how that leads to x̂=1, while explicitly confronting the mistake “best-fit equals exact fit.” Then connect back to the normal-equation viewpoint A^T A x̂ = A^T b (without adding new machinery): confirm that the computed x̂ satisfies it.
