body.q: If a matrix P satisfies P^2 = P, does that automatically mean it is an orthogonal projection?
body.a: No. P^2 = P only guarantees P is a projection. For an orthogonal projection, you also need symmetry in the real case, namely P^T = P.

slides.title: Why orthogonality matters
bullets: Two vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero.
Nonzero orthogonal vectors are automatically linearly independent.
An orthonormal basis makes coordinate and distance computations simple because basis directions do not interfere.
slides.speakerNotes: Start by tying orthogonality to computational simplicity. Emphasize the definition via dot product first, then mention the independence consequence and why orthonormal bases help.
slides.altText: Three bullet points: orthogonality is dot product zero; orthogonal nonzero vectors are independent; orthonormal bases simplify coordinates and distance.

slides.title: Orthogonal projections as “closest points”
bullets: The orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace is the closest point of the subspace to that vector.
If v is a vector and W is a subspace, then the projection Pv is in Im(P) when P is the projection onto W.
The residual v − Pv is perpendicular to the subspace in the orthogonal projection setting.
slides.speakerNotes: State the closest-point characterization and connect it to perpendicular residuals, staying aligned with the kernel facts. Keep the “perpendicular residual” as a consequence for orthogonal projections.
slides.altText: A vector projected onto a subspace with a closest-point interpretation and a perpendicular residual.

slides.title: From independent sets to orthogonal bases (Gram–Schmidt)
bullets: The Gram–Schmidt process converts any independent set into an orthogonal (or orthonormal) set spanning the same subspace.
Orthogonal spanning means the same subspace directions are present but without interference.
slides.speakerNotes: Use this to motivate why orthogonality is usable in practice: you can build an orthogonal basis for a span when you know it is independent.
slides.altText: Diagram-style description: Gram–Schmidt turns an independent set into an orthogonal set spanning the same subspace.

slides.title: Projections as linear operators: P^2 = P
bullets: A linear operator P is a projection iff P^2 = P.
If P is a projection, then v = Pv + (v − Pv) where Pv lies in Im(P) and v − Pv lies in Ker(P).
So the projection splits every vector into an “image part” and a “kernel part”.
slides.speakerNotes: Focus on the algebraic characterization P^2=P and the decomposition v=Pv+(v-Pv). This sets up the geometry used later for least squares.
slides.altText: A projection operator P splits any vector v into two parts: one in the image and one in the kernel.

slides.title: Orthogonal vs general (oblique) projections
bullets: P is an orthogonal projection iff P is symmetric (P^T = P) and P^2 = P.
For an orthogonal projection, Ker(P) = (Im(P))^⊥.
For a general (not-necessarily-orthogonal) projection, the perpendicular relationship need not hold.
slides.speakerNotes: Contrast the special symmetric case with the general case. This directly prepares students to avoid incorrect perpendicular assumptions.
slides.altText: A comparison: orthogonal projections give Ker(P) equals the perpendicular complement of Im(P), while general projections may not.

slides.title: Worked example: projecting b onto a column space
bullets: Let A = [1; 0] and b = [1; 1] in R^2.
The column space of A is the x-axis, so the orthogonal projection of b onto Col(A) is x̂ = [1; 0].
The residual is b − Ax̂ = [0; 1], whose dot product with any vector in Col(A) is zero.
slides.speakerNotes: Concrete geometry-to-algebra example. Students can see closest-point behavior and the perpendicular residual directly in coordinates.
slides.altText: Example in R^2: A has column space the x-axis; projecting b=[1;1] gives Ax̂=[1;0]; residual [0;1] is perpendicular to the column space.

slides.title: Least squares setup for inconsistent systems
bullets: The least-squares solution of an inconsistent system Ax = b minimizes the length of the residual b − Ax.
The least-squares solution x̂ satisfies the normal equations A^T A x̂ = A^T b.
Geometrically, Ax̂ is the orthogonal projection of b onto the column space of A.
slides.speakerNotes: Connect the minimization statement to normal equations and to the projection viewpoint. Keep it conceptual before doing any heavy computation.
slides.altText: Three connections: residual-length minimization; normal equations; geometry as projecting b onto the column space of A.

slides.title: Uniqueness when columns are linearly independent
bullets: When the columns of A are linearly independent, A^T A is invertible.
If A^T A is invertible, the least-squares solution is unique.
So independence of columns gives a single best-fit answer.
slides.speakerNotes: Use the invertibility fact to justify uniqueness. This is an important practical check when deciding whether the best fit is well-defined.
slides.altText: A note that independent columns make A^T A invertible, which yields a unique least-squares solution.

slides.title: Common pitfalls to watch
bullets: Orthogonality is defined by dot product being zero, not just “perpendicular lines in a picture.”
A projection preserves membership rules: vectors already in the subspace are unchanged by an appropriate projection.
Least squares minimizes residual length and generally does not make Ax̂ equal b.
slides.speakerNotes: Address three likely errors explicitly. These are the misconception corrections: picture-based orthogonality, projection changing the subspace, and least squares implying exact fit.
slides.altText: List of three pitfalls: orthogonality definition, projection behavior, and least squares not forcing Ax̂=b.

slides.title: How this all connects for solving problems
bullets: Least squares chooses Ax̂ as the closest point to b inside the column space of A.
Orthogonal projection ideas explain why the residual is perpendicular to the column space in the least-squares geometry.
Normal equations provide the algebraic way to compute x̂.
slides.speakerNotes: Close the loop: start with geometry, use projection properties, and end with normal equations as computation. Emphasize that orthogonality is the mechanism behind the best fit.
slides.altText: A final integrative diagram: column space, projection of b, perpendicular residual, and normal equations to compute x̂.

body.text: Welcome to Week 14: how we do a comprehensive review that actually matches the final exam. We’ll focus on (1) recognizing inconsistency vs infinitely many solutions, (2) reading solutions from row-reduced echelon form, (3) subspaces/basis/dimension from definitions, and (4) matrix algebra facts (order matters, inverses/determinants) that show up in multiple problem types.

Final-exam mindset: for any claimed result, we verify it by substituting back into the defining relations (e.g., check Ax=b, check that a proposed inverse satisfies AB=BA=I, check a projection satisfies P^2=P). We also practice “transfer”: take a new system or a new matrix, not a copied worked example.

Worked example (row reduction to classify solutions): Take the augmented system x + y = 1 and x + y = 3. When you row-reduce the augmented matrix, you end up with a contradiction row like 0x + 0y = 1 (equivalently 0=nonzero), so the system is inconsistent and has zero solutions. This is exactly the distinction behind the statement: “A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet.”

Rapid mixed drills (compute + justify): short sets on (a) pivots/basic/free variables, (b) vector-space/subspace tests using the zero vector + closure under addition/scalar multiplication, (c) independence tests via dependence relations, and (d) least-squares/projection residual facts. Students choose an answer first, then we confront common misconceptions explicitly.

Wrap-up: a checklist you can carry into the final—consistency classification (0/1/inf solutions), reversibility of elementary row operations, pivot positions come from echelon structure, vectors/subspaces are defined by axioms (not geometry), rank is pivot-count after row reduction, and determinant/inverse are about invertibility/volume scaling—not entry size.

body.markdown:
### Week 14 Comprehensive Review: quick definitions + what to watch for

**Core definitions to recall fast**
- **Solution of a system**: assign values to variables so *every* equation holds simultaneously.
- **Consistent vs inconsistent**: consistent = at least one solution; inconsistent = no solutions.
- **Row reduction + pivots**: elementary row operations (swap, scale nonzero, add multiple) are **reversible** and **preserve the solution set**; pivot positions come from echelon form during elimination.
- **Subspace**: a subset that (1) contains the **zero vector**, and (2) is closed under **addition** and **scalar multiplication**.
- **Span**: all linear combinations of a set of vectors; the span is always a subspace.
- **Linear independence**: only the “all-zero coefficients” combination gives the zero vector.
- **Basis & dimension**: basis = independent + spanning; **dimension** = number of vectors in any basis.
- **Rank**: dimension of the column space (number of pivot columns) after row reduction.
- **Eigenvector/eigenvalue**: **Ax = λx** with eigenvector **nonzero**; λ found from **det(A − λI)**.
- **Projection**: P is a projection iff **P^2 = P**; for orthogonal projections, Im(P)=Ker(P)^⊥.
- **Least squares**: minimizes residual length; Ax̂ generally differs from b (closest isn’t equal).

**Misconceptions to watch for (high-frequency)**
- “Every system of equations has a solution.” (Wrong: some are inconsistent.)
- “Row operations change the solutions.” (Wrong: they are reversible and preserve the solution set.)
- “Vectors are only 2D/3D arrows.” (Wrong: any object satisfying vector-space axioms counts.)
- “Any subset of R^n is a vector space.” (Wrong: must include 0 and be closed under addition + scalar multiplication.)
- “Matrix multiplication is entrywise and commutative.” (Wrong: product uses row–column dot products and order matters.)
- “Zero determinant implies the matrix is zero.” (Wrong: determinant zero means singular, not necessarily the zero matrix.)

**Self-check prompts (answer without notes)**
1) A system has two distinct solutions over the reals. Must the solution set be finite? Explain.
2) Given a row-reduced matrix, how do you decide which variables are basic vs free (and what determines pivot columns)?
3) Is a line in R^3 that does *not* pass through the origin automatically a subspace? Why or why not?

### If you missed the reading
If you didn’t follow the Week 14 review guidance, focus on definitions first and then compute. For systems, always classify into 0/1/inf solutions via row reduction and remember “parallel lines never meet” corresponds to inconsistency. For vector spaces/subspaces, never rely on pictures: use the zero vector + closure axioms. For matrices, verify inverse/projection claims by substituting into the defining equations (e.g., AB=I, P^2=P).

body.prompt: Pick one topic you feel least confident about, then describe how you would verify your final answer by substituting into the defining relations (for example, verifying a claimed Ax=b solution).
body.tension: The final exam rewards correct procedures and clear intermediate steps, but many mistakes happen when students move on without performing a defining check.
followUps: What exact definition are you using at each step, and where could that definition be tested directly?
If your computation produces a surprising structure statement, what consistency check would you do next?
Which misconception do you tend to fall into, and how will you recognize it early while working?

body.task: Solve a short mixed set that includes one systems-of-equations problem solved by row reduction and one matrix computation problem that uses the definition of AB entries. Then answer a justification question that asks you to state which of the possibilities for the system holds (zero, one, or infinitely many solutions) and why. Finally, verify at least one of your computed results by substituting it back into its defining relation.
steps: Solve the given augmented-matrix system using row reduction, and read off the solution(s) from the pivot structure.
Compute the required matrix product(s) by using the row-by-column dot product definition for each (i,j) entry.
State the system’s solution count category (zero, one, or infinitely many) and justify it using what the reduced form reveals.
Verify at least one computed result by substitution, such as checking Ax=b or checking AX=B for the claimed equation.

rubricBands.band: Correct procedure and clear intermediate work
rubricBands.observableBehavior: Student carries out elimination or matrix multiplication without skipping key steps and presents intermediate results in a way that matches the problem’s computational method.
